#4676. Why Living with Endometriosis May Double Your Odds of Migraine

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new analysis, researchers found females with endometriosis were 2.3 times more likely to also have migraine, and they said the two conditions may share a pain pathway involving nerves and inflammation.Recognizing that connection earlier could lead to coordinated care for both conditions, the researchers said.The analysis, presented at the American Neurological Association (ANA) Annual Meeting in San Diego on October 20, included more than 13 million females. The research hasn’t yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

Endometriosis occurs when tissue similar to what lines the uterus grows outside the uterus, Mallory Stuparich, MD, a gynecologic surgeon at MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, California, told Healthline. Stuparich was not involved in the study.Yohannes Woubishet Woldeamanuel, MD, lead author of the study and assistant professor of neurology at Mayo Clinic Arizona, told Healthline that migraine also involves more than one part of the body.“Migraine is more than a headache,” he said.Headache is one symptom, Woldeamanuel said, but migraine can also cause sensory, motor, and balance symptoms.“Migraine is a little complex. It’s a multiple-nervous system involving a condition,” he said.

Stuparich said endometriosis pain typically develops in 2 ways. The first starts in the lesions themselves.“There are inflammatory markers that are created by the endometriosis lesions themselves, and those inflammatory markers can irritate the nerves that live close by the lesions,” she said.The second involves the nervous system, Stuparich said. Scar tissue can grow its own nerve supply, and years of chronic pain can change how the nervous system responds. That adaptation can “perpetuate pain or make people feel sensations that normally wouldn’t be painful,” she said.Stuparich said the inflammatory and immune processes involved in endometriosis have “pretty significant overlap in the setting of migraines.”

One possible link between the two conditions is calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), a chemical messenger that helps transmit pain signals, the researchers said.CGRP plays a key role in migraine attacks, Woldeamanuel said, and blocking it reduces those attacks. CGRP medications work by blocking the sites where CGRP attaches or by binding to CGRP itself.Researchers have also found CGRP in endometriosis tissue.

A 2024 study published in Science Translational Medicine found CGRP in endometriosis lesions from both people and mice. In mice, blocking CGRP signaling reduced pain and reduced lesion size.

Other studies point to shared biology between the two conditions:

Stuparich said she was “not surprised at all” by the finding because it matches what she sees in her own patients.“We see this overlap of patients who have endometriosis also having migraines,” she said.Stuparich said the science still has gaps. She noted that nothing has been proven conclusively in peer-reviewed research yet, but the way both diseases behave supports a connection.“It makes sense that there would be overlap,” she said.

Endometriosis and migraine are treated by different specialists, so the overlap is easy to miss, Woldeamanuel said.For the analysis, researchers at Mayo Clinic Arizona reviewed 35 studies published over 50 years, comparing migraine rates among 207,675 females with endometriosis and 12,963,120 females without the condition.Short-term health records miss up to 90% of that overlap, according to the analysis. Migraine rates in females with endometriosis changed depending on how each study identified migraine.“This data is hiding,” Woldeamanuel said.

“These two clinics are siloed. One clinic doesn’t ask about the other condition. They just focus on their own specialty,” Woldeamanuel said.The findings of the analysis have not been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Some treatments already overlap, Stuparich said. Hormonal birth control “can sometimes be used to treat menstrually associated migraines,” she said.Stuparich said she has heard anecdotally of patients whose endometriosis symptoms improved after they started CGRP medications for migraine, though long-term data are still lacking.The researchers said the findings support studying whether existing CGRP-blocking migraine medications could also relieve endometriosis pain, potentially offering one treatment for both conditions.Woldeamanuel leads a planned Mayo Clinic trial testing one of those medications, rimegepant (Nurtec ODT), for endometriosis pain. The trial will also track migraine days in participants who have both conditions. It’s expected to finish in 2031, according to ClinicalTrials.gov.

People who suspect they have both conditions can take steps now to get them treated together, Stuparich said.Patients can raise the connection themselves, Stuparich said. She suggested a starting point for each appointment:

Patients can also ask for an early referral to the other specialist so both conditions get coordinated care, Woldeamanuel said. “The earlier it’s diagnosed, the better it’s managed,” he said.Stuparich said doctors are moving away from viewing endometriosis as only a gynecologic disorder because it can affect the whole body.“It is a whole body systemic neuroinflammatory neuroimmune disorder,” she said.

#4672. Can This Supplement Really Fight Inflammation? Here's What Doctors Say.

NAC promises it can improve your health and longevity. That might be a false alarm.

IS THERE ANYTHING NAC can’t do? Well, if you listen to the supplement industry, no, not really.

N-Acetylcysteine, or NAC, in its supplement form, has managed to accumulate a large number of alleged benefits in recent years. Depending on who you listen to, NAC supplements can allegedly boost your immune system, detoxify your body, improve cognitive function, increase energy levels, slow aging, increase fertility, reduce inflammation, prevent respiratory infections, and decrease oxidative stress.

That’s a whole lot of responsibility to place on one single supplement.

Add that to the fact that NAC is a proven medical treatment for a couple of specific diagnoses, and you have the perfect setup. Supplement companies can extrapolate evidence into claims that go way beyond current scientific evidence. That’s been a blessing and a curse for NAC manufacturers—and a legal headache that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) just made a major move to solve with the proposed creation of a new regulatory category just for NAC.

The legal maneuvering is complicated and, if finalized, would allow NAC to be considered a supplement but still a medical treatment which technically isn’t allowed—yet. Basically, there’s a lot to unpack here.

So what can NAC supplement do? And what even is NAC? Is it safe? Let’s break it all down.

NAC IS A sulfur-containing compound, a precursor of the amino acid L-cysteine. In medicinal or supplement form, NAC is converted directly into cysteine, which is then used to make and deliver glutathione, a powerful antioxidant that the body uses to scavenge free radicals and manage oxidative stress. (Yes, the body is a complex system.)

While NAC isn’t found in food, cysteine is readily available in animal proteins, legumes, dairy, nuts and seeds, and some vegetables. Compared to dietary cysteine, NAC supplements are a faster, more stable way of increasing glutathione levels.

NAC supplements are available in powders, capsules, liquids, and tablets. And while NAC has legitimate medical uses, it’s not officially FDA-approved as a supplement as of this second. Of course, this hasn’t stopped the supplement industry from selling it—or influencers from promoting it.

NAC has been in a weird legal gray area for years. Because it’s an actual medical treatment, it technically can’t be classified as a supplement, even though it’s often presented that way.

The FDA’s proposed rule would classify NAC as the first-ever “Dietary Ingredient Not Excluded from the Dietary Supplement Definition.” Basically, it will be allowed to span the categories of supplement and medication, which has never been done before. If finalized, this ruling would “provide for the lawful use of certain ingredients in dietary supplements that would otherwise be excluded from the dietary supplement definition,” per an FDA constituent update.

The proposed rule would allow products that contain NAC to be lawfully marketed as dietary supplements, as long as they’re not otherwise in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act). In theory, this may eventually apply to other supplement-ish ingredients; Right now, this is centered around NAC.

The proposed rule is open for public comment for 60 days. It’s not clear when the FDA when issue a final rule.

This won’t really impact the general public if it’s finalized. Instead, it clears up potential legal issues surrounding NAC. “This will more formally allow sales of NAC over the counter, without a prescription,” says Jamie Alan, PharmD, PhD, a professor of pharmacology and toxicology at Michigan State University in East Lansing.

While some members of the MAHA movement have pushed for this, Alan says it’s also a case of “well, why not.” She explains, “It is generally safe, and I agree with that assessment. It is also being sold as a supplement already so, why not?”

Alan stresses that this move doesn’t suddenly legitimize all NAC supplements or claims surrounding them. “If you are buying a supplement, you aren’t necessarily guaranteed that the bottle contains what it says it does,” she says. “There really isn’t evidence yet in my opinion that supplementing with NAC as a dietary supplement will be life-changing for the vast majority of people.”

NAC is the standard treatment for acetaminophen (Tylenol) overdose. High levels of acetaminophen deplete the liver of glutathione, which is required for the body’s detox pathways. If you’re curious about the geeky scientific mechanism: Quickly repleting glutathione by way of an intravenous NAC infusion helps clear the excess metabolites from the overdose and prevent liver damage.

NAC is also a mucolytic, meaning it can break down thick mucus in the respiratory system. (Yum.) While recent research found that NAC may help with with COPD and chronic bronchitis feel less worse, more investigation is needed to clearly establish effects and benefits.

WELL, NOT ALL that much. Other scientific trials have looked at NAC’s effects on conditions including mood and compulsive disorders, Alzheimer’s, Schizophrenia, and chronic pain. Overall, results have been mixed and largely unremarkable. For most of these conditions and disorders, larger-scale clinical trials are still needed.

So while it’s true that research does exist on NAC and wider health benefits, most of the new research trials examining NAC’s effects use doses that are far higher than what the average person would take, and in forms that are not available to the public.

This hasn’t stopped wellness influencers from broadcasting that NAC supplements can help heal whatever ails you.

Many of these influencers argue that because glutathione may reduce oxidative stress, NAC is amazing for longevity and anti-aging. It’s simple, they argue: Because oxidative stress is associated with aging, increasing glutathione with NAC supplements slows biological aging.

Except raising levels of glutathione in the body does not necessarily translate into a desired outcome. Science agrees: There is no long-term human evidence that showing that this suppresses oxidative stress to the level of having a clinically meaningful outcome. Taking NAC for “healthy aging” is more marketing than anything else at this point.

FOR MOST HEALTHY people, NAC supplements appear to be safe in doses between 600 milligrams (mg) to 1800mg per day. However, doses on the higher end of that range may have a higher risk of side effects such as gastrointestinal upset.

NAC is not recommended for people with clotting disorders. There are also some potential drug interactions between NAC and immunosuppressants, so it’s always a good idea to get a doctor or pharmacist to cross-reference any supplements with the medications you’re taking.

Again, remember that the supplement industry is largely unregulated. Always buy from reputable companies, and look for products that are third-party tested to ensure that what’s on the label is actually what’s in the bottle.

NAC has some legitimate—and even life-saving—medical uses, and research is constantly evolving. But what the supplements don’t have at this point, is compelling human evidence showing that NAC has any clinically meaningful effects in healthy people.

Abby Langer, RD is the owner of Abby Langer Nutrition, a Toronto-based nutrition consulting and communications company

#4671. Zonveer ZX3 review: one of the best-value electric dirt bikes for beginners

The Zonveer ZX3 is one of the best values I’ve seen in electric off-road riding, and one of the most fun things I’ve ridden to date – value for the dollar. Its Black Friday sale brings the 2,800W electric dirt bike down to $1,299, $500 off its $1,799 list price.

For that money, you get a 1,200Wh battery, dual hydraulic disc brakes, and full suspension in a 130 lb package. That’s a great entry point for beginners.

Zonveer is a young brand. It launched in the US in March with two bikes, the kid-sized DX1 and the ZX3, and it’s run by United Mobility, which lists its address in Dover, Delaware. It sells direct and ships from US warehouses, and Zonveer also sells the ZX3 across Europe under its own brand through its EU store.

Here’s what the ZX3 brings, according to Zonveer’s product page:

A hub motor means there’s no motor chain to maintain, and the NFC card and PIN unlock mean there’s no app to fight with. I like that.

Zonveer sent me a ZX3 to test, and I’m impressed with what they shipped, knowing the cost. It isn’t trying to be a race bike. And it doesn’t need to be. Here’s my first ride review:

With 2,800W peak, it’s somewhat modest by e-moto standards. That’s exactly what makes it approachable for someone who has never ridden a dirt bike: the power is enough to have a blast on trails without being intimidating.

My girlfriend had never ridden a dirt bike before, and she got comfortable within a few minutes, and she was hooked as soon as she got the hang of it.

And while testing with my girlfriend, it was clear this bike makes the most sense for lighter riders. Zonveer claims it climbs slopes of up to 30 degrees, which is optimistic for anyone over ~175 lbs, like myself. It still climbed some of the worst slopes on my land, but it did so with some difficulty, which wasn’t the case for some of my lighter friends who also rode it.

Range is the other claim to take with a grain of salt. Riding 45 miles on 1,200Wh means using under 27Wh per mile, which is e-bike efficiency on a 130 lb dirt bike with knobby tires. It’s still a lot of energy, and you can ride this long distances at lower speeds. Just expect less if you ride it hard, and that’s where the fun is at.

Zonveer’s Black Friday sale has the ZX3 at $1,299, and the company gave Electrek readers the code ELECTREK for an extra 5% off, which brings it down to $1,234.05.

The sale also includes a free water bottle and lock, and can be combined for a two-pack of ZX3s for $2,599. Shipping is free, the warranty is one year, Zonveer told us it accepts returns within 30 days on bikes ridden less than 10 miles, with a $200 restocking fee. Here’s the full refund policy.

We’ve ridden a lot of electric two-wheelers, and the ZX3 is one of the most fun per dollar. At $1,299, or about $1,234 with our code, it’s hard to find another 1,200Wh electric dirt bike with dual hydraulic disc brakes and full suspension from a brand that ships from US warehouses.

It’s not fast by e-moto standards, and the range and climbing claims are optimistic. But for beginners, and especially lighter riders, the power lands right in that sweet spot of manageable fun. It’s a bike you can learn on without scaring yourself, and it’s cheap enough that a family can buy two for less than one Sur-Ron.

#4669. ADHD Medications May Help Ease Menopausal Brain Fog

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Medications commonly used to treat attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may help reduce certain symptoms of menopausal brain fog, according to a review presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The research suggests that both lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) and atomoxetine (Strattera) may improve self-reported executive function in perimenopausal and postmenopausal people. However, they showed little to no effect on objective cognitive tests.

While this scoping review showed promising results, experts caution that it may be too early to begin recommending these medications to females experiencing menopause.

Sara Vaughn, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Clair Health, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are interesting and hypothesis-generating, but they do not yet establish ADHD medications as a treatment for menopausal brain fog.

Many middle-aged females report experiencing forgetfulness, slow thinking, reduced concentration, and difficulty finding words. This is often referred to as “brain fog,” and is a common occurrence during various stages of menopause.

These symptoms of brain fog also mirror the symptoms of ADHD.

Brain fog may be due to declining or fluctuating levels of estrogen during perimenopause, which affects dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus. This can impact memory, focus, and executive functioning.

Despite how disruptive these symptoms can be to quality of life, there is currently no medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to manage them. This often leaves clinicians in a position of trying to differentiate between brain fog from menopause and undiagnosed ADHD.

The review analyzed five studies involving females ages 45–60 with their last menstrual period within the past 10 years. The studies all focused on how ADHD medications affect outcome measures of cognition and ADHD severity.

The researchers found that with lisdexamfetamine, scores on the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared with 29.8 with a placebo. With atomoxetine, BADDS scores decreased from 38.6 to 25.5, compared with 30.1 with a placebo.

There was no significant benefit observed on objective cognitive tests (ex., memory and processing speed).

These findings suggest that certain ADHD medications may improve perceived cognitive symptoms during menopause, although benefits were not demonstrated on objective cognitive tests.

Jennifer Tat, a medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Sciences Center and lead author of the study, noted, “In the population data, symptom severity, not a formal ADHD diagnosis, predicted menopausal burden. Many women were never diagnosed, so relying on a chart diagnosis misses the women most at risk.”

“We have evidence that the menopause transition is associated with measurable brain changes,” said Vaughn. “But no specific brain signature of menopausal brain fog has been established. To study it rigorously, we first need to define what the term means and measure it consistently.”

Limitations of this review include the small number of studies and the small sample sizes. Most of the measures were also self-reported, which leaves room for error.

Also, the FDA has not approved these types of medications for menopausal brain fog, meaning using them for these purposes would be off-label.

“ADHD medications are not without risks, and I think it is too early to use them routinely for menopausal ‘brain fog,’” said Vaughn.

ADHD medications can carry risks, including cardiovascular side effects. Stimulants such as lisdexamfetamine also have the potential for misuse and dependence. These medications should only be used with medical supervision.

“I am a strong proponent of treating the underlying disorder rather than treating isolated symptoms. ADHD and menopausal cognitive symptoms may look alike, but that does not mean they share the same underlying mechanism—or require the same treatment,” noted Vaughn.

Further research, including additional long-term prospective studies, is needed before clinical guidance can be changed

“We hope this opens up the conversations with patients and providers. We recommend clinicians to screen patients for ADHD and, for those who screen positive, refer them to our psychiatric colleagues who have the knowledge and resources to perform a diagnostic test so that those women who have gone undiagnosed with ADHD can get the treatment they need and deserve,” said Tat.

According to the National Council on Aging (NCOA), your brain requires exercise to function optimally, just like your muscles do.

Ways to help keep your brain sharp and manage menopausal brain fog include:

The NCOA also suggests keeping your brain well-exercised by:

You can also speak with your healthcare professional about how menopause, estrogen levels, hormone therapy, and modifiable risk factors like a sedentary lifestyle or high blood pressure can affect cognitive health.

“I want clinicians to know that they must take brain fog seriously. Ask whether the symptoms are new or a lifelong pattern that menopause has worsened. ADHD in women often goes unrecognized for decades,” said Tat.

Tesla has pulled the $41,990 Model Y All-Wheel Drive from its US online configurator. The cheapest dual-motor Model Y you can order now is the Model Y Premium AWD at $49,990, an $8,000 jump.

The trim lasted just over nine months. Tesla launched it in early February, and it’s gone without a word from the company.

Here’s what Tesla’s US Model Y design studio lists as of today (prices before the destination fee):

When Tesla launched the base Model Y AWD in February, it was basically the stripped-down Model Y with a second motor. It had 294 miles of range, did 0-60 mph in 4.6 seconds and kept the same cut-down cabin as the base RWD. At a $2,000 premium over the single-motor version, it was the most sensible AWD pricing Tesla had offered in years.

And the AWD trim isn’t the only change. In February, the Premium RWD cost $44,990 and the Premium AWD cost $48,990. Both are now $1,000 higher.

Add it up and the cheapest all-wheel-drive Model Y went from $41,990 to $49,990 in nine months. That’s a 19% increase.

The timing isn’t great for Tesla’s competitive position. Chevrolet’s 2027 Equinox EV LT 1 AWD starts at $40,295 before destination, with 307 miles of EPA range. Ford’s Mustang Mach-E Select AWD starts at $40,795.

Both now undercut Tesla’s cheapest AWD crossover by more than $9,000.

If you live somewhere it snows and you were shopping for a new Model Y, the math just got a lot worse. You can still find some base AWD units in Tesla’s inventory, but once those are gone, that’s it.

This is also the latest cut in a year of Tesla shrinking its lineup. Elon Musk killed the Model S and Model X in January to free up Fremont for Optimus, and Cybertruck production is winding down. Meanwhile, the most recent new Tesla is the $61,990 Model Y L, which sits at the top of the range, not the bottom.

We liked this trim. It was the first time in a long time that Tesla treated all-wheel drive as a $2,000 option rather than a huge upsell bundled with a nicer interior, and it put the Model Y right in the price bracket of the Equinox EV and Mach-E with AWD.

Now it’s gone, and the Premium trims went up $1,000 on top of that. Tesla didn’t explain either move. It rarely does anymore.

There are two plausible reasons. Either Tesla is tight on Model Y build slots and would rather fill them with higher-margin Premium trims, or the cheap AWD simply wasn’t selling. We don’t know which. But both explanations land in the same place for buyers: a more expensive Model Y.

Tesla is not going to keep 6 different model Y trims especially when the most expensive trim in the Model YL is selling. They will definitely squeeze out as much money from selling more expensive trims so the lowest end trim will most likely be next to go.

And Tesla has a habit of this. The “Standard” name for its cheaper Model Y and Model 3 lasted a few months. The single-motor Cybertruck, the only version that made sense, was gone within days. Cheaper trims show up, get a news cycle, and quietly disappear.

That’s a problem for a company whose consumer lineup is shrinking down to two cars. The Model Y is Tesla’s volume. Thinning it out at the bottom is the opposite of what you’d do if growing EV sales were the priority.

How long before the $39,990 RWD goes the same way?

#4666. 15 Best Artificial Christmas Trees of 2026, Tested in Real Homes

Even though your holiday tree (probably) only comes out once a year, choosing the right artificial Christmas tree for your home is important to set a truly festive vibe. If you’re already committed to the faux lifestyle or are just dipping your toes in, the perfect tree is out there for you and your priorities. Maybe you want something bold and full of personality like the iconic Rockefeller tree in New York City. Perhaps you’re looking to go classic with a full lighting system included or something to match your favorite wreaths. No matter your preference, there’s a good chance that once you go faux, you’re never going back to the real deal. After all, there’s no watering involved, cleanup is a breeze, and easy storage is usually part of the design.

Our list below includes pre-lit trees that take the guesswork out of nostalgic spruces and even an enticing winter white design. And to really achieve a professional-looking holiday home, we’ve tapped experts like Kendall Jenner’s holiday floral designer Jeff Leatham and AD-darling designer Shea McGee for exclusive tips on how to level up any faux tree.

Reviewer: Divya Viswanathan, VP, commerce portfolio lead

This big, beautiful tree is inspired by the Fraser Fir. Known for its rich, dark green coloring and full silhouette, this tree is native to the Appalachian Mountains and has the distinction of being the type of tree most often used as the official White House Christmas tree.

To be honest, we can’t tell the difference between Balsam Hill’s faux version and the real thing. BH's impressive “true needle” foliage features 40 variations of branch types throughout and the effect is incredibly realistic.

The tree is available just about any height and light variation you could want, all of which feature an easy plug system. Easy plug trees have all the light strands plugged into the center pole, so all you have to do is place the three sections together and plug the tree into an outlet. There’s no need to ever unplug or take off any light strands.

The style pictured above is “color + clear,” which allows you to switch between multicolored lights and white lights via remote. For pre-lit trees with a single lighting style, there is an attached foot pedal to turn the lights on and off. The Twinkly light style features built-in app-controlled smart lights from Twinkly.

This beauty looks like it was plucked right off the tree farm, but all you have to do is just pull it out of the box. Speaking of, let your tree breathe for a day or two after you take it out of the box. That way, the branches can fluff up on their own before you decorate the tree. The tree features hinged branches, making setup and teardown straightforward (just push each hinge down and pop into a storage bag). If you’re looking for a large tree, and a full tree but don’t want to spend a fortune, this is a good, solid pick from The National Tree Company. The National Tree Company has been making holiday trees and decorations for more than 60 years, and they have plenty more styles to choose from on Amazon and Wayfair.

Reviewer: Stewart Savin, senior SEO analyst

Like a real-life Douglas Fir, this faux tree is designed to have a darker hue than other evergreens. Its needles are also longer and flatter than other evergreen varieties, growing out on either side of each branch rather than all the way around it.

Reviewer: Pujah Shah, global director of audience development, analytics & social

King of Christmas is a holiday-focused brand in the business of memory-making, with a vast inventory of artificial trees, garlands, and decorations to get your home in the Christmas spirit. The brand provides helpful written guides on assembling, shaping, and storing your tree, as well as video tutorials for a more visual learning experience. King of Christmas also donates thousands of trees to underprivileged families and communities impacted by natural disasters each year. The brand’s pre-lit Alpine Fir, a species native to Washington state, feels like spending the holidays in the Pacific Northwest, and allows you to enjoy festive vibes minus the maintenance. While pricing leans on the higher end, each faux tree is handcrafted to mirror the distinct shape, color, and growth pattern of real branches.

Another one of the prettiest pre-lit Christmas trees is this Blue Spruce. The full foliage on this fake tree includes realistic needles in blue-green and silvery hues paired with light brown stems, just like an authentic Blue Spruce. Like all Balsam Hill trees, it comes with an off-season storage bag, protective gloves to use while shaping the tree branches, and extra bulbs.

Reviewer: Brie Schwartz, commerce director Glamour

Another tried and true, super affordable option straight from Amazon. We appreciate our contributor Brie Schwartz’s approach to the fake tree game. Instead of spending big bucks going for a super realistic tree, she aims for over-the-top flocking and lots of lights to lean into the fact that she prefers the faux variety (and to have her tree up for as long as humanly possible for the season). Go big or go home, right? If Schwartz’s approach rings true to you, too, this might be the perfect tree for your household.

Reviewer: Kate McGregor, commerce market editor

We’ve turned to Quince time and time again for their high quality, yet affordable bedding and soft goods over the years. This artificial spruce is the newest addition to our catalog of tested items from the brand. (Fun fact: It’s even the main image of this story in case you were wondering which faux tree made it as our model this year). Quince’s take on a spruce employs an interesting branch design: The back end of each limb features bushier evergreen bunches while the front-portion presents tips that look more realistic. This clever system actually makes the tree look more lush from within while still maintaining the appearance of something life-like on the surface. Commerce market editor Kate McGregor noted in her review that the tree did give off a fuller look, and was especially handsome once decked out with a merrily maximalist slate of ornaments from some of our favorite holiday hubs like John Derian and Anthropologie. Just be mindful that the more realistic branch segments can leave a semi-sticky residue on your hands (an issue you’d have with real tree too, we might add).

Reviewer: Lauren Arzbaecher, commerce producer

Let us set expectations here: For a tree that’s under $100, you are probably not going to find the highest quality option for your Christmas tree. That said, we wanted to put one to the test to see how it held up in person. If you are looking to prioritize price over super realism, we think this option makes a lot of sense.

Reviewer: Stewart Savin, Senior commerce SEO analyst

Unconventional tree colors—like gold, silver, or white—are smart options if your taste favors a non-traditional Christmas tree. It brings all the drama but doesn’t pretend to be something it’s not. This all-white Kingswood fir tree won’t dampen any pastel-forward design schemes in the way something with a more authentic evergreen look might. Plus, the snow-like white needles provide a neutral canvas for making your ornaments stand out. Tester Stewart Savin liked that the slim design of her seven foot-tall selection can fit into more narrow crevices, though it’s available in seven-and-a-half, nine, and 12-foot options with wider diameters. A disciple of Kathy Hilton’s design philosophy—that every room deserves a unique tree set up during the holiday season—Savin plans on keeping the Dunhill Fir from the Holiday Isle she tested last year as her main tree, and this smaller silhouette with “winter wonderland vibes” in her bedroom or sunroom.

How easy was it to assemble your tree (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? Given that artificial trees are, by their very nature, annoying, I’ll give this an 8 overall. The [storage] bag it arrives in is a little awkwardly wrapped, and the entire set is kind of heavy, but it’s a really intuitive assembly process and could easily be done by one person. The pieces snap in place with very little effort. The big time suck is fluffing up the needles and zhuzhing the branches until it looks full. The entire process from bag to completely assembled took about 10 minutes.

What was the quality of the tree packaging? Will you be able to store your tree for future years? The bag is a little flimsy, but that’s my only gripe. It fits well and isn’t too bulky to stow in the small basement storage unit in my New York apartment. I imagine I’ll easily be able to store the tree for its entire lifespan.

How long did it take to fluff and prepare your tree? Did you see a lot of needle loss in the process? It took about five minutes of fluffing to get the tree to look real. The branches were pretty flexible and held their shape well. No needle loss at all!

Did your tree come with lights or decor? If so, how easy was it to install? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? N/A

How easy was it to assemble your tree (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? 6

What was the quality of the tree packaging? Will you be able to store your tree for future years? The tree was packaged well in a cardboard box, and I’ll definitely be able to store it in the box at the end of the season.

How long did it take to fluff and prepare your tree? Did you see a lot of needle loss in the process? The most time-consuming part of the assembly process was unfurling and fluffing the tree, but there was very minimal needle loss. I spent about 40 minutes setting it up but roughly 35 minutes of that was fluffing the many sections. The lights that came already incorporated into the tree were twisted around each section very tightly, so I had to spend a good amount of time untangling the lights so that I could fully fluff it up.

Did your tree come with lights or decor? If so, how easy was it to install? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the easiest)? The tree came pre-lit, which is nice, but as I said, the lights were wrapped so tightly that it took a bit to loosen them so I could fluff the tree. I’m giving it an 8 since it did save some time that it came pre-lit, but it wasn’t totally seamless.

Did your tree live up to your expectations and was the size accurate? Yes, it definitely lived up to my expectations! I specifically wanted a slimmer tree so I wouldn’t have to rearrange my living room too much, and this was the perfect width. The 7.5-foot height is perfect for my tall ceiling, and the tree is slim but still full and realistic-looking so it doesn’t look gangly.

How full is the tree (scale of 1-10, with 10 being the fullest)? 6—since the tree is intentionally more slim and compact, it’s not luxuriously full, but once fluffed up, you can’t see any of the inner metal parts that might make it look artificial otherwise.

How realistic is the tree? (on a scale of 1-10, with 10 being the most realistic)? 6—up close, you can see that the needles are plastic, but the overall fullness and structure of the tree make it look authentic otherwise. The metal components that make up the frame are hidden in the interior column, which definitely helps. The base is metal and clearly artificial, but I always put a skirt around my tree (even when I’ve had a real one) so that aspect is also naturally concealed.

Puleo International is another well-known name in the artificial tree game, selling at outlets like Amazon, Wayfair, Home Depot, and Lowe's. The brand’s slim Fraser fir was exactly what tester Emma Tubbs was after: “I wanted a slimmer tree so I wouldn’t have to rearrange my living room too much, and this was the perfect width,” she says. The tree’s versatile look and approachable price point also helped it overtake the Best Choice Products Pencil Christmas Tree for our ‘Best Slim Tree’ pick. “The 7.5-foot height is perfect for my tall ceiling, and the tree is slim but still full and realistic-looking so it doesn’t look gangly,” says Tubbs.

We always research products thoroughly before including them, and test every single one. Our reviews are thorough, in-depth, and honest. We put ourselves in the shoes of the shopper (because most of the time, we are the ones shopping!), and make sure that we’re answering the questions that we would want answered in the buying process.

We favored natural-looking trees that are easy to set up. We also took shipping into account and tested trees that arrive not only in style, but with speed.

All trees that were reviewed were unboxed, set up (and lit up) by our contributors. They lived with trees and experienced all they had to offer firsthand, so that they could share the real deal with our readers.

What Size Christmas Tree Is Right for Me?

First and foremost, the height of your fake Christmas tree should depend on the height of your ceiling. A good rule of thumb is to keep your tree at least one-and-a-half feet lower than your ceiling, otherwise, it will look crowded. “I like to leave about six to12 inches between the top of the tree and the ceiling, so it feels intentional, not squeezed in,” says Shea McGee (more on the designer’s holiday advice below). Both McGee and Jeff Leatham, the floral designer who helped mastermind Kendall Jenner’s festive holiday house, agree that seven to eight feet hits a sweet spot in most homes. “The goal is balance: A tree that feels full and joyful but still lets the room breathe,” says McGee.

Some people want to avoid the hassle (and extra cost) of buying a fresh tree each year, while others are allergic to real trees or are concerned about the fire safety hazard that comes along with real trees (they can become highly flammable as they dry out). Others (including people with pets) know that a real Christmas tree can be bait for disaster. Fresh or faux is really a matter of personal preference, and anyone who wants a fake Christmas tree should go for it. Leatham points out that in faux trees, the branches don’t drop, the coloring stays vibrant, and there’s often more structure to add extra ornaments.

Is It Better to Get a Pre-Lit Tree Or to Do It Yourself?

Choosing if you want your tree pre-lit is one of the first decisions you’ll make when navigating the vast artificial tree world. Pre-lit options are the preference of holiday decor gurus like Leatham. “Always, always, always go for prelit—it makes the tree look more full and realistic,” he tells us. Our editors like that pre-lit Christmas trees are convenient to set up (opposed to blindly garlanding string lights) and how they help guarantee your lighting scheme will look uniform. That said, drawbacks include potentially difficult repairs. While you can easily unstring removable lights to troubleshoot, built-in LEDs might pose bigger technical issues. On the other hand, stringing your own lights may be a more complex, time-consuming process, but you’ll ultimately have more control over which areas of your tree are spotlighted.

How Should You Decorate Your Christmas Tree?

You’ve gotten your tree up, fluffed the branches, and poured yourself a nice cup of hot cocoa or eggnog to celebrate—now comes the fun part: decorating. While there’s no right way to decorate your Christmas tree, we looked through our archives for some tips and tricks to give your setup some extra sparkle.

If your mentality is “more is more,” your holiday hero will be Kathy Hilton, who greeted AD back in 2021 with four artificial Christmas trees decked out with all the bells and whistles (emphasis on the bells). One tip we’d steal from Hilton is the idea that the decorations don’t have to go up all at once. “I normally start decorating in October, then keep adding until December,” says Hilton.

Kendall Jenner, on the other hand, favors a more traditional tree, dipped in nostalgic classics like tinsel, twinkle lights, and vintage Christopher Radko ornaments that were passed down by her mother, Kris. Her designer reveals that she even loves stringing popcorn for the tree and dried orange slices on garlands. “Every year, more and more of my clients want more traditional holiday decorations that they can invest in, collect, and pass on to other generations,” says Leatham. “I love that idea of seeing the same ornaments every year and having them bring back wonderful memories.” Since we have a feeling you have your own collection of heirloom Christmas decorations that have been collecting dust, we’d look to the supermodel for inspiration.

Color scheming your ornament display is one way to set yourself apart from the pack. “Red and green are traditional Christmas colors, but I love to break away from tradition and use bright jewel tones to create a dramatic and sophisticated look for the holiday season,” says Annie Sloan, color expert and creator of Chalk Paint. Stylist Dorcia Kelley of Kelle Miles Studio also suggests using a planter instead of a traditional tree stand or skirt for a modern look. “When hanging ornaments, you want to make sure you’re hanging it towards the end of the branch instead of right at the tip. This way, they’ll be more stable,” she says.

We also recommend playing with shapes, textures, and finishes to create as much interest as possible. AD’s perfect Christmas tree (pictured at the top of this article) features lots of vintage-inspired John Derian ornaments that bring on the kitsch, accented with classic ball ornaments in a range of sizes to create depth and dimension. A color palette of muted blue and bold metallic hues complement the deep green branches while slivers of silver tinsel add holiday pizzazz.

Fluffing your artificial Christmas tree is the key to convincingly faking the real thing. Most of the time, your tree will arrive with all the branches up-turned straight out of the box, and you’ll first want to mount the tree in its stand or collar. Next comes the actual fluffing—as reviewer Pujah Shah mentioned, it’s a smart idea to wear some work gloves to avoid any pricking that might occur while you’re working through the branches. Starting at the bottom, you’ll fan the largest branches down, layer by layer, until you reach the very top (where the branches become much shorter). If your branches have smaller tips built in, we like the center-right-left method of starting toward the base of the tree and positioning the smaller tips first center, next towards the right, and lastly towards the left, until you’ve reached the end. After that, you’ll go branch by branch, noticing that your tree looks full and much more lush with each adjustment. Afterwards, all that’s left to do is make any minor fixes to eliminate bald spots and voila!

What’s the Best Real Christmas Tree to Buy?

Again, that’s completely a matter of personal preference. Trees come in a variety of hues, some with a dark green, some with a blue tint, and others with a bright shade. Some have spiky needles while others are soft to the touch. Trees vary by geographical region and what's native to your area, but some of the most popular options used as Christmas trees across the U.S. include the Fraser Fir, Balsam Fir, Douglas Fir, and Blue Spruce (all of which are available in faux varieties, as well!).

How Does the Lifetime Cost of a Faux Tree Compare to Annually Buying a Real Tree?

While how much your real Christmas tree costs will vary depending on its size as well as where you live in the United States, expect to spend anywhere from $40 to well over $100. In a few years, that running total will start to cost you, but with an artificial tree, you’ll pay the total cost up front. High-quality trees can also last you up to 15 years, making the sometimes extravagant price tags more digestible, especially in the later years when you’re no longer burdened with figuring out the logistics of strapping that netted Douglas Fir onto the car roof.

Flocking refers to the process of dusting your artificial Christmas tree with a powdery white overcoat to mimic the appearance of fresh snowfall. Some trees—like the Yaheetech tree Brie Schwartz tested—come pre-flocked, but if you prefer a DIY moment, ready-to-flock sprays are also available at most big box retailers. We like Balsam Hill’s guide to flocking your tree, which details a recipe for homemade flocking, as well as all the safety precautions you’ll want to take: Like wearing protective gear, flocking in a well-ventilated environment, and ensuring you’re using non-hazardous materials. (Though if your budget allows, we think it might be best to invest in one of the brand’s ready-flocked trees.)

In the grand scheme of artificial Christmas trees, King of Christmas and Balsam Hill are widely known as the crème de la crème, thanks to their realistic appearance, convenient setup, and thoughtful extras like complimentary storage bags for the off-season. While both fall into the category of more luxuriously-priced holiday decor, Balsam Hill’s price points are slightly higher ($349 to $4,000+ while King of Christmas ranges from $229 to $3,000+).

In our own quests for the most elite faux trees, we’ve also tried both brands. Commerce vice president Divya Viswanathan called Balsam Hill’s Fraser Fir “the Christmas tree of my dreams,” while contributor Andrea Lewis previously called her Blue Spruce from the brand “a lovely addition to our holiday traditions—elegant, easy to manage, and captures that cozy, Christmas air perfectly.” AD’s global director of audience development Pujah Shah became a King of Christmas convert last holiday after testing the brand’s Alpine Fir tree. “I wanted something tall, sleek, and a little bit dramatic that felt intentional in a modern space but still cozy enough for family chaos—it nails both,” says Shah. We think that both brands are great options—it’s hard to beat how realistic Balsam Hills designs are, and holiday floral designer and one of our experts, Jeff Leatham even named King of Christmas as his favorite brand. To choose the right brand for you, we recommend figuring out what will suit your space and your decorations, as well as establishing a price point you’re comfortable with.

We tapped the designer and creative force behind one of our favorite interior brands, McGee & Co., on the best ways to make your artificial Christmas tree really pop this season. Read on for her advice on how to make merry with a beautiful, yet intentional holiday set up.

Is There Such a Thing as an Ideal Sized Christmas Tree?

“When you’re choosing a tree, the ideal size really depends on your space. I like to leave about 6–12 inches between the top of the tree and the ceiling, so it feels intentional, not squeezed in. For most standard spaces, a 7-7.5-foot tree hits the sweet spot. If you have tall ceilings, you can absolutely go bigger—9-12 feet fills the volume beautifully. And in smaller rooms, a slimmer silhouette keeps things festive without overwhelming the layout. The goal is balance: A tree that feels full and joyful but still lets the room breathe.”

What are Some of the Design Benefits of Choosing an Artificial Christmas Tree Versus a Real One?

“I love the flexibility an artificial tree gives you. You know exactly what shape and fullness you’re getting, and the branches stay right where you want them—which makes decorating so much easier and more polished. They also hold up all season long, which is great if you like to decorate early. And of course, you can reuse them year after year, which means you can invest in the style you love and bring it back every holiday.”

How Do You Make an Artificial Christmas Tree Look More Realistic?

“Start with a tree that already has a natural, realistic base—good branch texture goes a long way. From there, keep your palette cohesive so the whole tree feels curated instead of busy. I love layering garlands because they add that organic movement you see in real trees. Then finish with meaningful ornaments, ribbon, and a few organic touches—like dried citrus or pinecones. Those add warmth and authenticity, making even a faux tree feel beautifully lifelike.”

“Both options have their place. A pre-lit tree is all about ease—the lights are perfectly placed, and you get that warm glow the minute you plug it in. It’s great if you want a beautiful tree without the extra steps. An unlit tree gives you more creative freedom. You can layer different styles of lights, change the mood from year to year, and really customize the look. It takes a bit more time, but it can feel incredibly intentional. So, if you want quick and polished, go pre-lit. If you love the process of styling every detail, unlit is the way to go.”

The easiest way to make your artificial Christmas tree look like a real tree is to, well, cover it up. Go heavier on the decorations this year: Think garland, Christmas lights, pinecones, ornaments, a tree topper, etc. We're talking the works. Check out our go-to holiday decor tips that will make the best Christmas trees look even more magical.

It’s affordable in bulk, doubles as a garland, and covers quite a bit of real estate from low to high. And who doesn’t love a bow? We pulled an option to satisfy the minimalists as well as some embellished trim that’s got major maximalist appeal.

A dead giveaway—no pun intended—that your tree’s a fake is the base: that plastic, mechanical-esque tree stand. Cover that metal stand up with a festive tree skirt (or basket!) as you would with real Christmas trees.

If your tree doesn’t have pre-strung lights, head to the holiday aisle for some white or multicolored lights. Some of our favorites include unconventional and more delicate-looking lights that don’t necessarily scream “Christmas.” They’ll draw the eye to the center of the tree and take the attention off of the branches. Besides, you can never have too many lights in your home decor during the holiday season.

When scouting out ornaments for your tree, look for options with serious heirloom potential. Kendall Jenner’s Christopher Radko’s classic ornament collection is a good example—and Etsy sellers have troves of vintage ornaments to start your own traditions or recreate the supermodel’s holiday style. These miniature bulbs we found at Terrain are a fun way to create more depth when paired with larger balls, and we like that the different colors really pop when your tree is lit. We also turned to John Derian for gorgeous, traditional options pictured on our tree.

#4665. 16 Best Strength Training Exercises to Build Muscle and Strength Fast

There’s no shortage of strength training exercises to pepper into your muscle-building routine. If you’re a regular on FitTok, you might’ve noticed that a new exercise seems to pop up regularly. So, which ones should you pepper into your routine?

“It all comes down to your goal,” says Angela Gargano, a trainer and creator of Strong Feels Good & Pull-up Revolution. The exercises you fill your program with are your most important tools for success.

Keep reading for the best strength training exercises to try, exactly how to add them into a total-body routine, and expert-backed tips for making a plan that works. Ready to get lifting?

Build lasting strength with the WH+ Strong Over 50 Plan, here

Below, we’ve rounded up some of our favorite strength training exercises, spanning all the different muscle groups. Here’s how to create a well-rounded full-body routine you can do regularly.

Equipment: Dumbbells, kettlebell, resistance band | Good for: Total body Instructions: Pick one move from each category—push, pull, hinge, lunge, squat—to create a total body workout. Do it two to three days a week, preferably on nonconsecutive days. For each move, do the allocated amount of sets and reps, resting for 1 to 2 minutes between sets. Select weights that make the last few reps challenging, but doable (and more on selecting weights, below!).

Alternatively, you can split up muscle groups if you have multiple days a week to work out (if you’re working out only two days a week or less, stick with a full-body plan). There are a few ways to do this. If you're planning on strength training twice a week, you can also opt to do one upper-body day (the push/pull exercises) and one lower-body day (the hinge/lunge/squat exercises). Select four or five exercises with a variety of exercise type (don’t fill a lower body day with only squats, no matter how much you love them!) to create your workout.

Or, if you're working out three times a week, you can split your workouts to do one push/pull day, and two hinge/lunge/squat days, or vice versa, depending on what part of your body you want to strengthen most. If you're training more than three times a week, you can split by muscle group.

Here are 16 of the best strength training exercises to fill in your workout.

Why it rocks: Pushups are a classic move for a reason: They work your chest, shoulders, and triceps. Another perk? They engage your core muscles and build functional strength.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 or 4 sets of 8 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Unlike a standard shoulder press, this upper-body exercise challenges all three muscle heads of your deltoids.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Triceps extensions are killer for isolating and strengthening your triceps muscles for improved strength and functionality.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: You’ll strengthen your lats, traps, and delts with this classic upper-body pull move. The bent-over position provides a little extra challenge to your core, too.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps.

Why it rocks: This is an excellent bent-over row variation that targets your lats and rhomboids, requiring less core stability than a traditional bent-over row.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: You’ll strengthen your lats, traps, and delts with this upper-body movement. “This exercise is so beneficial because you are working in a hinged position and teaching your body how to properly brace,” Harvey notes. “This will come in handy the next time you need to bend over and pick something up.”

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps.

Why it rocks: Deadlifts build overall strength and power in the posterior chain muscles, including the hamstrings, glutes, and lower back.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 6 to 8 reps.

Why it rocks: This move strengthens your lower body while also improving stability, and the resistance band is great for added intensity.

Sets and reps: Aim for 2 or 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps each side.

Why it rocks: This beginner-friendly move works your glutes, core, and lower back, and may help mitigate back discomfort due to sitting.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 8 to 10 reps.

Why it rocks: Reverse lunges work the quadriceps, hamstrings, and glutes, all while improving coordination and stability.

Sets and reps: Aim for 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps each side.

Why it rocks: Curtsy lunges torch the glutes and outer thighs, while also improving lower body strength and muscle symmetry.

Sets and reps: Aim for 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps each side.

Why it rocks: In addition to working your outer glute muscles and upper legs, this move helps promote stability and balance in your lower body.

Sets and reps: Aim for 2 to 3 sets of 16 reps alternating.

Why it rocks: Holding an object like a kettlebell (though you can also use a dumbbell) at chest height calls your core more in on the action—training your body proper core activation that will allow you to push heavier as you get stronger.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 8 to 10 reps.

Why it rocks: The Bulgarian split squat can shore up functional strength unilaterally, helping to correct any imbalances.

Sets and reps: Aim for 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps each side.

Why it rocks: This move improves single-leg balance by promoting unilateral strength. Plus, it's easily adaptable since you can change the height of the step and the weight you're holding.

Sets and reps: Aim for 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps each side.

Why it rocks: With a wider stance than used in a traditional squat, this move builds quad and glute strength, and also increases hip mobility.

Sets and reps: Aim for 3 to 4 sets of 8 to 10 reps.

Strength training can help you build and maintain muscle mass, improve your joint and bone health, support better body composition, and even increase your longevity. And, including it in your routine is easy to do, as long as you follow these tips and tricks.

“The biggest thing in putting together your entire workout is making sure that you have a proper warm-up, always, no matter what,” says Gargano. “People tend to throw that out the window but dynamic moves are going to help you wake the body up a little bit before you get into your strength training.”

To execute a proper warm-up, select 3 to 4 dynamic and mobility exercises (these are a few of our favorites!) and do them for 30 seconds apiece, 2 or 3 times through. If you're planning on exercising a specific part of your body that day, make sure your warm-up is tailored to that (e.g., if you're about to do a leg day lift, select a few warm-up moves that promote blood flow to the lower body, like lateral lunges or the World's Greatest Stretch).

“In your programming, there’s a combination of things you should always have,” says Gargano, noting you don’t have to put them all in the same workout/day, but they should certainly all fit in your week: Push movements (like pushups and chest presses), pull movements (like pull-ups and rows), squats, lunges, and hinge movements (think: deadlifts, hip hinges).

Programming your workouts will largely depend on how many times a week you work out (more on that here). The more times a week you can exercise, the more you can split your workouts by muscle group. For example, if you're working out three days per week, you might be interested in doing one upper-body day, one leg day focused on glutes and hamstrings, and another focused on quads and calves. If you're only working out twice per week, you'll want to make sure you're programming for the whole body: at least one upper-body lift and one lower-body lift.

“I know people are going to be like, ‘Well, what about my core?’ but your core is used in all those movements,” Gargano assures.

“You want to be sure that you're working all the body parts so that you're not uneven,” says Gargano. It's an issue trainers see a lot—people focus so hard on defining one part of their body that they neglect the rest. For example, if you're aiming to build up your glutes, don't only do hip thrusts on lower body day. Incorporate some lunges and squats in there, too, to strengthen your quad muscles so they can work in tandem with your strong glutes.

As long as you hit all five of the main movement patterns we named earlier (push, pull, squat, lunge, hip hinge) throughout the week, you should be in good shape.

A few weeks into your workout program, your body will get used to what you’re doing—so you'll need to level up the challenge, “so that your body can continue to develop and work the muscles in different ways,” says Gargano. That means increasing your weights, reps, or sets to progressively overload the muscles—doing so will help them get continuously stronger, and ensure your performance never plateaus.

To know when to up the weights, use the two-for-two rule: Once you can do two extra good-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load. From there, try to increase 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. But remember, this is just a recommendation—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

The best exercise plan is the one you're going to stick to. And the one you're going to stick to is the one that best fits into your schedule.

“You need to figure out what is working well for you and your body,” says Gargano. “Everybody's different, so try out two days a week first, and then if you feel good, maybe add that third day.”

Once you have your schedule set, don't feel like it's an end-all, be-all. The more you can hit your workouts, the better—but there's no reason to knock yourself down if things get busy and you miss one or two. You can always abbreviate your workout by cutting a few exercises or sets, or get moving by going for a brief walk. The key is to stay moving as much as you can. It won't always be perfect, and that's okay.

#4664. Meta to deploy 25 electric semi trucks across I-10 corridor, but has nothing to ship

Electric truck operator Nevoya is expanding its deal with Meta with the fresh deployment of 25 Class 8 battery-electric trucks on the Interstate 10 (I-10) between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona … but Meta won’t be shipping any products.

The second major trucking deal between Facebook parent company Meta and electric truck operator Nevoya will put 25 new battery-electric semis on I-10, running freight between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona. But Meta isn’t buying trucks, hiring drivers or shipping its own products. Instead, Zuck’s company helping pay for someone else’s cleaner freight through environmental attribute certificates (EACs), a carbon credit mechanism that lets companies claim the emissions benefits of electric trucking without operating the trucks themselves.

“Coming back to Nevoya for a second corridor reflects what we look for in our value chain work: partners that can scale, and agreements we can repeat, said Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta. “Freight is part of the emissions footprint of building and operating our data centers, and multi-year commitments like this help address our scope 3 emissions and make electric trucking available and competitive on the routes that serve the regions where we build.”

Meta was one of several buyers in the DC-based Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) buyers’ alliance. The group’s collective EAC purchases supported Nevoya’s initial 63-truck deployment on the Houston–Dallas corridor back in May. This new Agreement, however, is a standalone deal between Nevoya and Meta only, and gives Meta an established framework to open more electric truck corridors in the future.

This clever application of these agreements is what makes the Dallas-Houston run stand out, with GMA calling it, “the first large-scale application of book and claim to zero-emission trucking.” The company adds that this arrangement helps client companies overcome existing barriers to EV adoption while enabling Nevoya to deploy new trucks, “where they deliver the strongest commercial and operational value.”

Yuck. That's the feeling I get when reading this. Am I happy that more EV semi's will be going on the road? Yes. But the way it's being done just makes me feel dirty. And I refuse to do or have anything that Mark Zuckerberg is involved with. I find him to be disgusting. But then again I find most of these super wealthy people to be vomit inducing.

So I'd liken this deal to a guy who goes out to a bar with the sole intention of "having some fun". And it doesn't matter to him how that happens, as long as he gets his happy ending. But then when the sun rises and the darkness vanishes, who this guy slept with is revealed and it's not good.

Zucherberg isn't doing any of this for the planet. He's doing it for money.

Nevoya expects Meta’s fresh batch of semis to begin prowling I-10 in 2027, where they’ll cover approximately 4 million freight miles annually.

#4663. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.
