#4661. Here are the coolest e-motorcycles and gear we saw at EICMA 2026

Every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase. That means that all of the newest electric motorcycle announcements happen in one place, and we get a chance to check out the coolest developments and most interesting new gear.

Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.

LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the company has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.

The new S4 Honcho family was a major focus, including the street-oriented Honcho Street, off-road Honcho Trail, and newly unveiled Honcho Skate, a stripped-down addition to the modular platform. The booth also included LiveWire’s larger S2 electric motorcycles, creating a pretty broad spectrum from lightweight urban machines up through full-size highway-capable electric motorcycles.

The other big piece of the booth was DUST Moto, which LiveWire acquired earlier this year. The production-intent DUST Hightail was displayed alongside the newly revealed DUST Spur, giving LiveWire an immediate presence in the increasingly popular lightweight electric dirt bike category.

Add in STACYC’s electric balance bikes for young riders, and the entire booth almost looked like an electric two-wheeler progression chart: start a kid on a STACYC, move up through lightweight DUST and Honcho machines, and eventually graduate to a full-size LiveWire.

GR1T Motorcycles is a relatively young European electric motorcycle startup that caught my eye at EICMA with its G1 platform, a lightweight electric motorcycle designed and engineered in Italy. The basic recipe is pretty compelling: 130 km/h (81 mph) top speed, 11 kW of continuous power and 26.6 kW (36 hp) peak, all while weighing just 130 kg (287 lb).

Perhaps most importantly for urban riders, its roughly 6 kWh battery is actually split into two removable 3 kWh packs, meaning apartment dwellers can pull the batteries out and charge them inside. They’re big, but removing them is doable.

GR1T’s bikes therefore pack in around 50% more battery capacity than most electric motorcycles in this size and weight class, meaning roughly 50% more range, as well.

There are also some interesting and clever design choices, like the underslung rear suspension and the triple-camera system that includes front and rear dashcams plus a cockpit-facing camera for recording the rider.

The clever part of the overall design scheme is that GR1T isn’t developing a separate platform for every motorcycle. The same basic G1 chassis, motor, batteries, belt drive, and electronics underpin four versions: the G1S Street, G1X Scrambler, G1XR Raider, and utility-oriented G1M Mission.

Prices are set to start at €8,495 including VAT, putting these squarely in that emerging category of reasonably affordable, lightweight electric motorcycles that have enough speed for real-world commuting without chasing superbike performance.

There’s an important caveat, though: these aren’t production motorcycles yet. GR1T says it is currently fundraising, with factory development and pre-orders set to follow after funding closes and first deliveries now targeted for the first half of 2028.

So the bikes aren’t quite ready for primetime yet, but it’s definitely a company to watch.

Real Motors brought one of the more visually striking electric motorcycles to EICMA with Project: ARES, a futuristic electric café racer that the American startup describes as an “Electric Analog” machine – basically an attempt to preserve the raw, mechanical connection of motorcycling while ditching unnecessary screens and gadgetry.

And there’s plenty of performance underneath the sci-fi bodywork: Real Motors lists a 75 kW (100 hp) motor, a 15 kWh battery, a 120 mph (192 km/h) top speed, and an estimated weight of 485 lb (220 kg).

The analog analogy is spot on, with the display probably the simplest and most straightforward I’ve ever seen on an electric motorcycle. There’s also no app, no subscription, and no digital handcuffs. The bike is very much the electric equivalent of a simple ICE bike that just rides, albeit with a much nicer ride.

Unlike many of the futuristic concepts scattered around EICMA, ARES is actually headed toward limited production.

Real Motors plans to build just 250 examples in its first LOT 01 production run, with pricing starting at $20,000 and North American deliveries targeted for early 2027. European deliveries are expected after homologation is completed.

The company has also brought former LiveWire CTO Vance Strader onto the project as it makes the difficult transition from a very cool prototype into an actual production motorcycle.

I actually had the chance to do a spin on the bike, and so I’ll be reporting back on the experience. But you can tell from my smile below that the ride was quite an experience!

Seatylock has been my go-to e-bike lock company for several years now, and I use their locks for my several e-bikes and my wife’s e-bike too.

Now Seatylock has returned with some even more impressive locks. The company showed off its new Ultra D28 lock, which is both angle grinder-proof and wide enough to lock the wheel of a motorcycle. It solves the problem of how do you make a lock strong enough for a motorcycle but also small and light enough that you can actually carry it with you, unlike a massive chain lock that usually stays where you park your motorcycle overnight.

In the image below, you can see the shackle next to an exposed section demonstrating the diamond coating that essentially destroys angle grinder discs – even diamond coated discs.

The company also has a slightly smaller version of the same lock designed for bicycles.

Both will absolutely destroy even the toughest angle grinder discs. Sure, eventually someone could cut through them, but it may take a dozen discs and by that point the thief has moved on to an easier target.

At EICMA 2026, Royal Enfield continued expanding its electric motorcycle ambitions with its Flying Flea sub-brand, showcasing the scrambler-style motorcycle alongside its growing lineup of lightweight, retro-inspired electric motorcycles.

There were several interesting colorways and customized designs on display, showcasing the Flying Flea’s stylish design.

The new models blend Royal Enfield’s classic design heritage with modern electric technology, targeting urban riders and those looking for a fun, approachable electric motorcycle rather than a high-performance machine.

With distinctive styling, compact proportions, and an emphasis on accessible riding, the Flying Flea lineup represents Royal Enfield’s effort to carve out a place in the emerging market for smaller electric motorcycles while maintaining the character that has made its gasoline-powered bikes so popular.

Yamaha showed off its new NMAX E electric scooter, bringing battery-powered performance to one of the brand’s most recognizable urban scooter families.

Designed as an electric alternative to the popular gasoline-powered NMAX, the new model combines familiar sporty styling with a quiet, low-maintenance electric drivetrain aimed at everyday city commuting.

The NMAX E uses Yamaha’s new compact eAxle powertrain, shared with the larger-wheeled XENTER E, and delivers up to 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power, putting it in the 125cc-equivalent class.

With its practical step-through design, automatic operation, and approachable performance, the NMAX E represents another step in Yamaha’s push to electrify its urban mobility lineup, particularly in European markets where scooters are already a popular alternative to cars.

Segway showed off a new vision for safer electric scooters, including its futuristic X Cruiser concept that takes rider protection to a whole new level.

Rather than relying solely on traditional motorcycle safety equipment, the X Cruiser explores automotive-inspired features such as integrated seats with seatbelts, partial enclosures, and even a fully roofed version designed to offer additional protection from the elements.

The concept includes several configurations, ranging from a more conventional open scooter to a partially enclosed design and a fully covered model that looks like a cross between a motorcycle and a tiny electric car. While these designs are still concepts rather than production-ready scooters, they demonstrate how Segway is rethinking two-wheeled transportation by exploring ways to make electric scooters safer, more comfortable, and potentially more appealing to riders who might otherwise be hesitant to trade four wheels for two.

Eli Electric Vehicles took to EICMA 2026 to display its compact Eli Zero electric quadricycle, a tiny two-seat urban EV designed to offer much of the convenience of a car without the size, weight, or expense of a conventional automobile.

With its enclosed cabin, side-by-side seating, and ultra-compact footprint, the Eli Zero offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles for short city trips, combining the weather protection and comfort of a car with the maneuverability and efficiency of a much smaller vehicle.

The company revealed a more powerful L7e-class version of the Eli Zero that it had previously teased, expanding the vehicle’s capabilities beyond its existing L6e configuration. The new Race Edition also pushes the envelope farther with custom interior and a few extra accents to the body.

With growing interest in smaller, more efficient urban transportation, Eli’s presence at EICMA definitely underlined how the show is increasingly embracing electric mobility solutions that go beyond traditional motorcycles and scooters.

NIU showed off its latest lineup of electric scooters, continuing the brand’s push to make battery-powered two-wheelers a practical alternative to gasoline-powered urban transportation. Known for its sleek designs, connected technology, and approachable electric scooters, NIU highlighted models aimed at a range of riders, from everyday city commuters to those looking for more powerful machines capable of keeping up with faster urban traffic.

The company showed off several new models for the 2027 model year, with scooters that combine modern styling with features such as smartphone connectivity, smart security systems, and efficient electric drivetrains, all while maintaining the simplicity and low operating costs that make electric scooters so appealing.

While I didn’t see anything groundbreaking at the brand’s booth this year, the incremental updates look to push new tech features further throughout the brand’s many models, helping more of NIU’s offerings enter that premium level that the company has been known for.

For something a bit wilder, Honda shared its futuristic EV Outlier Concept, an electric motorcycle that explores what two-wheeled design could look like when engineers are freed from the constraints of traditional gasoline-powered motorcycles.

With its long, low-slung profile, radically different riding position, and futuristic bodywork, the EV Outlier looks more like something out of a science fiction movie than a conventional motorcycle. The concept features electric motors integrated into both wheels, giving it two-wheel drive while opening up new possibilities for packaging and weight distribution.

Rather than simply replacing a combustion engine with a battery and motor, Honda used the EV Outlier to rethink the entire motorcycle layout, demonstrating how electrification could lead to entirely new types of riding experiences.

While the bike remains a design concept with no announced production plans, it offers an intriguing glimpse into Honda’s vision for the future of electric motorcycles.

Vespa showed off its next-generation electric scooter lineup at EICMA, including electric versions of the Primavera, Sprint S, and Primavera Tech. While they don’t look radically different, there’s a lot more happening underneath the familiar steel bodywork.

A new Italian-made, rare-earth-free electric motor improves efficiency and performance, while the 45 km/h Primavera and Sprint S now feature removable batteries.

The faster 67 km/h Primavera Tech gets up to 90 km of WMTC range – a 12.5% improvement – along with an updated vehicle management system and more efficient charger.

FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More.

Micah Toll is a personal electric vehicle enthusiast, battery nerd, and author of the Amazon #1 bestselling books DIY Lithium Batteries, DIY Solar Power, The Ultimate DIY Ebike Guide and The Electric Bike Manifesto.

The e-bikes that make up Micah’s current daily drivers are the $999 Lectric XP 2.0, the $1,095 Ride1Up Roadster V2, the $1,199 Rad Power Bikes RadMission, and the $3,299 Priority Current. But it’s a pretty evolving list these days.

#4660. 5 Best Hotel Sheets for a Boutique Bedscape (2026)

We want to let you in on a secret: You can replicate the good night’s rest you get at luxury destinations by dressing your bed with the hotel-quality sheets. Aside from accessories like fluffy down feather pillows and mattress toppers, we often attribute cotton percale and sateen to a five-star sleep.

To get down to the nitty-gritty of these sheets, a hotel bed dressed in a percale weave boasts a crisp look and feel, almost as if it were made from your favorite pressed button-down shirt. A sateen weave, however, is polished and resembles the appearance of pearls. What’s more, both of these high-quality sheets have breathable, wrinkle-resistant qualities for a refined aesthetic we know and love in a high-end establishment.

Many of our favorite places to buy bedding—including Italian luxury brands like Frette—even create custom bed linens like these for the best hotels around the world. Scroll below for a staycation-style set of sheets.

For consistency, all of the prices reflect queen sizes. However, many brands offer twin size and king size options too.

The Andersen Hotel, a family-owned boutique retreat in Copenhagen, offers guests sheets, towels, and robes from the editor-favorite brand Boll & Branch. To mimic the experience at home, you can shop the entire collection, including the Signature Hemmed Sheet Set tested and beloved by contributor Rachel Fletcher. The buttery-soft cotton sateen set is made with long-staple cotton fibers, and only gets softer with each wash. “That extra-soft feel, paired with the lovely, cooling properties, makes them feel like the luxury sheets they are,” Fletcher shares. After more than five years with these sheets, Fletcher adds that there are no signs of pilling or wear, “just that coveted softness which feels lived-in but not worn out.”

Matouk is a legacy brand known for bespoke touches on high-thread-count sheets. Their hotel collection is found in a number of luxury resorts and historic inns, including Hotel Barrière Fouquet's in New York City and renowned Arizona wellness escape Castle Hot Springs. The Bergamo is their most lightweight percale sheet, combining Giza 87 and 92 Egyptian cotton yarns. “I hate scratchy sheets, and I breathed a sigh of relief when I slipped into these,” says contributor Allie Weiss. “They are lightweight, crisp-looking, and soft to the touch.” We also recommend taking advantage of their personalization feature, which allows you to add a monogram to the edge of the sheet. Just remember that each piece is sold separately, so you’ll have to build your own bedscape.

Another property with Frette bedding, The Palace Hotel in Madrid is an AD-favorite historic hotel. “You’ll definitely want to stop by La Cúpula during your trip for an afternoon drink and some bites from the stylish tapas menu,” says shopping editor Audrey Lee. “If it’s the right time of day, the room becomes drenched in sunlight through the dome-shaped stained glass ceiling.” As for the bedding, you can mirror the hotel’s lavish interiors with Frette’s bold sheets. The polished sateen set boasts a thick border in six color combinations to wake up a bedroom.

Make a statement without sacrificing a classic hotel look with this tuxedo sheet set. Crafted by Frette for the Ritz-Carlton, this design includes a white-on-white stripe pattern that is perfect for a suite-inspired space. For a unique touch, you can also pair a set of the classic pillowcases with this set for a blend of solid colors and bold lines. Instead of shorter threads that can fray over time, this fabric is made of extra-long staple cotton sateen for an ultra-soft and durable feel.

Priding themselves on a sustainable outlook toward hospitality, the 1 Hotel Group offers a connection with nature and serenity even in the heart of the city. With green-certified buildings and a focus on wellness, it’s no surprise that this hotel’s bedding is equally natural. Kassatex’s 100% cotton sheets are softer than percale but not as shiny as sateen. Contributor Kate McGregor stayed at the 1 Hotel Seattle and was impressed with the breathability. “I’m quite a hot sleeper, but even after a cross-country flight, I slept soundly,” she says. “There was no swishing noise as I moved, either, a pet peeve of mine with really crisp hotel sheets.” Machine washable and available in either a queen or king set, these sheets come with a 60-day trial, so you can really get a feel for them without worrying about a wasted investment.

What Type of Sheets Do Five-Star Hotels Use?

While it varies from property to property, the majority of the hotels on this list use white cotton sheets. Whether percale or sateen, the best hotel sheets all offer a neat, design-agnostic look that suits the center of New York just as well as the rolling hills of Tuscany. Percale will have an added crispness and cooling factor, while sateen will have an added shine and smoothness. Regardless of material finish, look for an all-natural fiber makeup (like 100% cotton) and a versatile white colorway.

Why Do Hotels Like to Use White Bed Sheets?

From an aesthetic perspective, white sheets offer a cloudlike, serene escape for the guest. They also look the cleanest. Stark white sheets cannot hide stains or wear and tear as darker colors can—you can see exactly where each thread has snagged. White bedding is also the most easily sanitized; it even has its own setting on your washing machine. Bleach is necessary to kill germs, especially in a commercial setting, and you don’t want to risk the color fading and yellow stains that can occur on colored sheets.

What Type of Sheets Does The Ritz-Carlton Use?

The Ritz-Carlton uses white cotton sheets from luxury bedding brand Frette. The extra-long staple cotton is more durable than short strands, proven wash after wash. Boasting a subtle monochromatic stripe, The Ritz-Carlton’s sheets play with texture without departing from the clean lines and opulent energy of their suites' overall design scheme.

What Fabrics Are the Best Sheets Made of?

Long or extra-long-staple cotton sheets are considered the “best,” in our experience. These typically have a smooth finish and hold up well over time. That said, so much of it comes down to your own personal preferences. “[Deciding] which one is best for a particular person or climate is relative,” Katie Glusica, professor in the fibers department at the Savannah College of Art and Design, previously shared. “A percale in the 200 to 400 thread-count range will be durable and have a cooler sensation and a lighter weight feel, best for people who run a little warm or where the climate is warmer. Sateen sheets in the 300- to 600-thread-count range are best for someone looking for softness over durability, and better for cooler climates where a heavier feeling sheet is more comfortable.” Then, there are the more seasonal fabrics like airy linen for summer or thick flannel for winter. If you’re still undecided, we often find that Goldilocks-level comfort in cotton sheets with thread counts between 200 and 600 threads per inch.

What Are the Best Bed Sheets for Hot Sleepers and Cold Sleepers?

While percale is recommended for hot or warm sleepers, compared to other cotton sheets, shopping writer Julia Harrison argues the best is bamboo or Tencel lyocell. “AD editors and I prefer these natural fibers because they usually feel cool and gentle against skin, but they also have great temperature regulating qualities since the fabric absorbs excess moisture to help you stay refreshed while you sleep,” she says.

And during the winter months, or for those who run cold year-round, there’s nothing more comforting than sinking into a bed dressed in flannel sheets. “These are great for keeping you cozy and toasty because of a brushed (and sometimes double-brushed) cotton material that feels soft to the touch,” says senior shopping editor Nashia Baker. “It depends on the brand, but some make their sheets with 100% long-staple cotton, like supima cotton, that’s known for its durability without wear over time.”

What Is the Difference Between Percale and Sateen?

Both are made from cotton, but the weave is what differentiates the two. “Percale is a classic one-over, one-under construction that creates a crisp, breathable fabric with a matte finish reminiscent of fine poplin shirting, while sateen’s longer thread float produces a smoother hand and subtle sheen,” Rebecca Weinstein, vice president of design at Highgate, the management company for the Atlas Hotel in Boston, previously told AD. Hot sleepers will feel most comfortable in cooling sheets like percale, while those who prefer a less structured, smooth feel will likely splurge on sateen. “Sateen is more dense, with more threads packed in, so the fabric is warmer,” shared Preeti Gopinath, associate professor of textiles and founding director of the MFA textiles program at Parsons School of Design in New York. “Percale is cooler, and with a thread count of 150 to 200, there is less fabric per square inch, which allows for better airflow.”

#4659. Lifting Heavy Isn’t the Whole Story When It Comes to Building Strength. Here's What to Do Instead.

My name is Cori Ritchey, and I am an exercise physiology nerd turned fitness journalist, and the fitness editor at Women’s Health. When I’m not writing, editing, and researching fitness, I’m teaching it to my personal training and group fitness clients. In my new column, Between Sets, I’m pulling back the curtain on the same advice, tips, and ‘aha!’ moments I share with my clients while they’re catching their breath. Stick around for the strategic, science-backed nuggets that’ll help you move better, train smarter, and actually enjoy the process.

Scroll any fitness feed and you’ll see it: people clanging plates, chasing PRs, and even pulling dangerous stunts for the pride of lifting heavy. And where there’s real joy in getting stronger, there’s also real pressure to keep adding weight.

As a strength and conditioning coach and the fitness editor at Women’s Health, I’ve been preaching the lift-heavy-or-go-home gospel for years. For valid reason: challenging your muscles over time is one of the most reliable ways to build lasting strength, support bone health, improve body composition, and stay functional as we age.

The “lift heavy” ethos isn’t new. Strength training is as old as Ancient Greece, where the first gyms were developed. It progressed through decades of physical culture into Muscle Beach, USA, the birthplace of American lifting that started as a beachside gymnastics park in Venice Beach, California, in the 1940s. It was there, too, where the first American women bodybuilders, like legendary Abbey Stockton, emerged—at a time when many scientists still believed lifting was bad for the body.

Research eventually caught up to what lifters were already experiencing: resistance training works. More women, especially in recent years, started showing up for it, too. In 2004, 17 percent of women reported regularly participating in weight lifting. By 2020, that number has bumped to nearly 30 percent. Then came the influencer era, amplifying a message that’s equal parts motivating and misleading: lifting weights is good for you—but it has to be heavy to count.

There’s a kernel of truth in there. Progressive overload (the process of gradually increasing the stress you put on your body in a workout) builds muscle and strength, and increasing load is an efficient way to do so.

And that matters—especially when heavier, heavier, heavier simply isn’t in the cards.

Because for many, it’s not. It requires access to specific equipment, time to train consistently without rushing through sets, and quality coaching and information to nail form and stay injury-free. It also has to be safe and appropriate for your body on any given day—whether you’re navigating chronic illness, postpartum or perimenopause realities, and injury history, or limiting pain. And even when everything lines up on paper, there’s a very real mental hurdle: walking into a gym and loading up a bar can be intimidating as hell.

Still, if you’re here to build strength, change your body composition, protect your bone health, or invest in your movement longevity, lifting heavier will certainly help—but it’s not the only path to lifelong strength. Somewhere along the way, “heavy” became synonymous with “effective”, and “light” or "moderate" became codes for “waste of time.”

The exercise research world is finding that’s not the case. “You don't need to do anything heavy for the health benefits of resistance exercise to take place,” says Stuart Phillips, PhD, kinesiology professor and hypertrophy researcher at McMaster University.

Adequate research has suggested that hypertrophy (the fancy scientific term for muscle growth) is not determined by a magic rep goal or the weight on the bar, says Susie Reiner, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, assistant professor of exercise science at Seton Hall University, and CEO of TheoryEx, a sport science research and consulting firm. “Instead, hypertrophy appears to be driven by whether a training set provides a sufficiently strong internal stimulus to the muscle, which is reasonably defined as effort and proximity to muscular failure.”

Trainers have traditionally been taught that specific rep ranges map neatly to specific goals: 1 to 3 for power, 3 to 8 for strength, 8 to 12 for muscle, and 12-plus for muscular endurance. But newer findings show you can build muscle across a much wider rep range—roughly as low as 5 and as high as 25, Phillips says. “There is, then, by definition, no sweet spot for muscle building, because the whole repetition range then becomes the sweet spot.”

Across several studies and meta-analyses, similar muscle growth has been seen between people who train with lighter loads (about 30 to 40 percent of their one-rep maximum), and those who train with heavier loads (about 70 to 85 percent of their one-rep maximum)—as long as sets are taken close enough to failure.

Muscle growth is dependent on recruiting and fatiguing a large portion of muscle fibers, Reiner says. Your muscles need a reason to adapt. With heavier weights for fewer reps, you recruit a lot of fibers immediately. With lighter weights for higher reps, you recruit them more gradually.

One thing to note here: while a large percentage of these studies have only been done in men, Phillips notes that “the work that has been done in women shows us that actually men and women respond very, very similarly to weight lifting in terms of muscle mass gain. Women have less baseline muscle, but relatively speaking, they gain the same amount as men—that's been robustly shown.” Phillips and his colleagues are currently running several studies (including one study specific to perimenopausal women!) that will further clarify what this looks like in women.

Researchers feel confident that as long as sets are taken sufficiently to failure (more on what that means coming up), different loading strategies can produce similar hypertrophy, Reiner says.

Here’s what that looks like IRL: Let’s say you have biceps curls on your workout plan each week. One week, you pick up the 10-pound dumbbells, and do 3 sets of 12 reps. In the sets, when you approach the end of that rep range, it feels tough—you can maybe grind out 2 more reps max. The next week, you reach for the 15s. You can only hit 6 reps before you feel like your form is faltering, but the effort feels similar—you’ve still got about two reps left before your form breaks down.

The heavier weight might feel more empowering, but both workouts deliver a similar muscle-building stimulus—assuming you’re training regularly enough, eating enough protein and calories, and adequately recovering, of course.

Sure, research confirms you don’t have to lift crazy heavy—but that doesn’t mean that coming close to failure feels easy. Failing a rep can be scary (and honestly, discouraging). Here’s the good news: you don’t need true, all-out failure. You just need to train to proximity to failure.

One practical way to gauge that is with the rate of perceived exertion scale. “Rate of perceived exertion (RPE) is a global effort scale, typically ranging from one to 10,” Reiner says. An RPE of 10 represents maximal effort—no chance you could do one more rep. A RPE of nine suggests you could do one more, an RPE of eight means you could probably do two more reps, and so on and so forth.

Muscle growth still occurs between RPE of 7 to 9, Phillips says. “You don’t need it to be a 10 out of 10 where you’re red-lining and can’t get the bar off your chest.” In other words: you can train hard without routinely hitting the point where things get sketchy.

That matters, because the closer you get to all-out failure, the more your injury risk can creep up—especially if you start twisting, bouncing, and compensating to force a rep you simply don’t have.

The failure you want to flirt with is technical failure, or technical fatigue. “Technical failure means you cannot complete another repetition with good form,” Phillips says—that’s where injury risk rises. Muscular failure (otherwise known as momentary failure) occurs when a muscle is unable to generate enough force to complete another rep, regardless of maximal effort. Picture trying to do one more biceps curl and you quite literally cannot lift your arm and the weight up again—that’s muscular failure..

Aim for technical failure. Pushing yourself too far in an effort to achieve muscular failure could cause your body to overcompensate and push you into a compromising position. The good news, too, is technical failure tends to be very close to muscular failure for most people, Phillips says.

A useful rule of thumb: stop when you have one to two perfect-form reps left in the tank.

Yes, you still need to reach for that RPE of 7 to 9—but there’s more ways to do that than just reaching for the next highest weight. Here are some other elements you can play with to up the challenge:

Frequency. Reaching for heavier weights, you can simply aim to reach for any type of weight more often. That might look like increasing your strength training days from two to three days a week.

Volume. Think of your training volume as the amount of weight total you lift during a given session. Sure, lifting heavier loads is one way to increase your total, but it can also be accomplished by increasing the amount of sets or reps you do.

Rest time. Decreasing the amount of rest you allow yourself gives your muscles less time to recover, wearing them out quicker with lighter loads.

Time under tension. The amount of time your muscles work for matters. Increasing your time under tension, or the amount of time your muscles are working in a lift (for example, lowering a curl for a slow four-count).

That all being said, heavier loads might still take the cake in terms of efficiency. You’ll find yourself increasing your frequency and volume to monotonous levels if you never increase your load.

Back to biceps curls: Say you get comfortable at six reps at 15 lbs. After a few weeks, it no longer starts to feel challenging for you, so you increase it eight. And then 10. And then 12. If you never reach for the intimidating 20 lb dumbbells, you’ll eventually find yourself having to do sets of 30 reps just to feel something. And that can become time consuming. You don’t need extremes all the time—but you do need your training to stay challenging.

“For individuals who are uncomfortable training to very high levels of effort, consistent training at moderate-to-high RPEs combined with sufficient volume and progression can still produce meaningful muscle growth,” Reiner says. “From a long-term perspective, hypertrophy depends less on any single maximal set and more on repeated exposure to challenging, well-managed training over weeks and months.”

Convinced to start pushing closer to failure? Here are a few ways to progress safely.

The two-for-two method is a classic progression strategy used by professional trainers. Once you can do two extra proper-form reps beyond your planned rep target for two workouts in a row, you’re ready to increase your load.

Let's use the biceps curl example just one more time. You’ve been training with the 15s for sets of 8, and now you can hit 10 with clean form for two workouts in a row. That’s your cue to grab 17.5s the next go.

How much should you increase, exactly? The National Strength and Conditioning Association’s guideline is 2.5 to 5 pounds for upper-body exercises, and 5 to 10 pounds for lower-body exercises. Reminder that this is just a general guide—you can do more or less based on how you specifically feel.

Trying heavier weights is way less intimidating when you have a safety net.

If you’re nervous, ask for a spot. Maybe you already have a gym buddy you workout with regularly that can help pull the barbell up if you get stuck on a bench press. If you don’t, ask one of your gym’s trainers or employees. Most people will politely oblige, and will even appreciate your effort in challenging yourself.

Have a conversation with your spotter before you get into the lift. Tell them how many reps you’re aiming for, and a cue you’ll give them when you want them to jump in and help (my go-to is a simple “now”—since that’s about all you can get out when you’re out of breath).

Some days just don’t feel as strong as others. Maybe you didn’t sleep super well last night, stressed about work, or are at a tough point in your cycle. That’s life. When that happens, you need to respect the cues your body gives you.

If your warmup sets feel unusually heavy, take the hint: this just might not be the day to pick up that heavy weight. It doesn’t mean you’ve regressing, it’s just a bump in the road. Strength, and muscle building, is not a linear process.

Build muscle with the WH+ Build & Burn series

Ultimately, building and maintaining muscle mass is one of the strongest investments you can make in long-term health—especially as you age.

And lifting heavy is one effective way to provide muscle-building stimulus to the body—but it isn’t accessible, comfortable, or safe for everyone all the time. The goal is progressive challenge, and lighter loads can deliver that when you train with intention and effort.

“You do not need to lift heavy to build muscle, but you do need to train with intention,” Reiner says. “The best approach is the one that someone can perform consistently, safely, and with enough effort to challenge the muscle over time.”

Cori Ritchey, C.S.C.S., is the fitness editor at Women's Health, as well as a certified strength and condition coach and group fitness instructor. She’s reported on topics regarding health, nutrition, mental health, fitness, sex, and relationships for several years. You can find more of her work in Men’s Health, HealthCentral, Livestrong, Self, and others.

#4658. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4657. Hyundai is overhauling the Kona, and it looks like it may still be offered as an EV after all

Hyundai is skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh and plans to launch a completely redesigned Kona, with a sleek new style and an updated high-tech interior.

It’s been nearly four years since Hyundai introduced the second-generation Kona, meaning, like most of its models, the compact SUV was expected to receive a mid-cycle refresh.

Hyundai is apparently going straight to the third-generation model instead. Earlier this year, early-stage prototypes were spotted in Korea that looked much boxier and more rugged than the current Kona.

Since then, several test mules have been captured testing in the US, Europe, and other regions, confirming the Kona will adopt a more upright, traditional SUV design similar to the new Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson.

The wider, more powerful design appears to draw inspiration from Hyundai’s off-road Crater Concept, revealed at the LA Auto Show last year.

Hyundai said the off-road SUV Concept was a preview of the “next evolution” of its Extreme Rugged Terrain (XRT) vehicles, such as the IONIQ 5 XRT and Palisade XRT Pro. Is the Kona next in line to receive the XRT treatment?

A post shared by SHORTS CAR (@shorts_car)

Apparent leaked images from a few months ago revealed a design that looked like a mashup of the Crater Concept and IONIQ 5, with pixelated lighting and a clamshell hood.

Most recently, the third-gen Hyundai Kona, codenamed “SX3,” was spotted disguised in a parking garage in Korea. The images were sent to ShortsCar, revealing the new Kona’s wheel design.

While earlier reports suggested Hyundai planned to drop the all-electric Kona variant and would only offer gas and hybrid versions, the prototype captured in Korea is expected to be the EV model. However, Hyundai has yet to confirm powertrain or battery specs.

The updates are even more evident on the inside. Previous spy images appeared to show the third-gen Hyundai Kona running Hyundai’s new Pleos Connect infotainment system, like the IONIQ 3.

In the IONIQ 3, Hyundai offers a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen, plus an optional driver display.

Like the current model, the third-gen Kona is expected to be available with fully electric (EV), hybrid, and gas-powered powertrains.

While Hyundai skipped the 2026 Kona EV, the electric version could return in 2027 or 2028 when the third-generation model is expected to arrive.

The hybrid version will likely use the same 1.6L hybrid engine as the new Seltos, while the EV variant could offer similar powertrain and battery options to the IONIQ 3.

The IONIQ 3 is available with two battery packs in Europe and the UK: 42 kWh and 61 kWh, offering WLTP ranges of up to 213 miles (344 km) and 308 miles (497 km), respectively.

#4655. The Secrets to Whole-Life Training

A well-rounded fitness routine that will enhance all of your activities and adventures starts with your feet.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There’s more to getting fit than chasing a PR or sweating through another bootcamp class. The real payoff? Being ready for the next workout, the weekend adventure, the everyday hustle, and all the years ahead.

The key is making different types of exercise work together, rather than relying on any one activity. This multifaceted and well-rounded approach to training means you’re working more than the muscles, because you’re focused on the movements.

When you approach training this way, you’re literally starting from the ground up. “Every single step you take, your foot is the first thing that hits the ground,” says Jen Perez, DC, a chiropractic physician who combines clinical practice and education to help people improve foot health and lower-body function. “It’s the first thing that interfaces with the world around you, what has to be strong and springy when you want to run or jump or dance or ski.”

A whole-life, well-rounded training plan comes down to five essentials, according to Courtney Conley, DC, a best-selling author and chiropractic physician with more than two decades of clinical experience:

Cardio and strength may already be part of your routine, but the others can be easier to overlook; especially because they deliver numerous movement benefits that you may not equate them with. For example, Conley emphasizes that power training isn’t just for athletes; it also has practical life applications. “Getting up and out of your chair, having good reaction time, and making sure you don’t fall if you step off a curb and trip are all part of that category,” she says.

Mobility means moving freely through a full range of motion, while balance helps you adjust to changing surfaces and react when your footing shifts—it isn’t just holding a tree pose. “There are thousands of nerve endings in each foot that help communicate to our brain where we are in space,” Perez explains. That feedback, combined with the feet’s ability to grip the ground, helps keep you steady.

Recovery is what allows your body to benefit from hard training, yet Conley says it’s often ignored: “I think one of the biggest mistakes is that people don’t recover.” Sleep, adequate nutrition, and lighter days that deliberately scale back workout volume or intensity give your body time to adapt and help you come back ready for your next workout.

The work you do in the gym should go beyond just trying to look good and prepare you for the demands of everyday movement. For strength and power work, Conley recommends deadlifts and kettlebell swings to train the hip-hinge pattern, along with farmer’s carries to build strength in the core and lower body. “I love all that functional movement,” she says. “A sled push is also great, because as your heel comes off the ground, you’re hitting all the intrinsic muscles of your foot.”

Certain machine exercises may not seem so functional but can address specific weaknesses. For instance, Conley says she often uses seated calf raises to strengthen the tissues around the Achilles and leg extensions to isolate the quadriceps. She also recommends plyometrics—quick, explosive jumping and hopping drills—to develop power. “Try double-leg and single-leg hops, forward and backward, side to side, and zigzag moves,” she says, recommending five or six sets of 10 reps per exercise for plyometric movements.

Ankle and big-toe mobility are number one on Conley’s priority list for things you should focus on outside of your regular workouts. “When you can’t propel through the ankle, you’re going to get there by extending the knee so you can push yourself forward,” she says. “People come in with knee or back pain when oftentimes it’s an ankle problem.” She suggests making mobility a regular part of the week rather than waiting until something feels stiff or restricted. Even a short dedicated session can help you maintain the range of motion your training requires.

Perez says your feet also adapt to the surface beneath you and absorb force. “If you think of your foot like a trampoline, every single step we take, whether walking or running, the foot needs to be able to lower, which is that mobility piece, then it needs to be able to spring back up.”

Perez recommends two simple drills to improve foot mobility and strength: the Foot Handshake, where you weave the fingers of one hand between the toes of the opposite foot and gently circle the foot at the ankle; and Lift, Spread, and Reach, where you lift all five toes, spread them apart, then reach them forward as you lower them.

Another way you can activate your feet during training is to choose your shoes wisely. When it comes to footwear, Perez has one non-negotiable regardless of the activity: a wide toe box that lets your toes spread naturally. “If your toes are more narrow than the ball of your foot, that tells me we’ve got some work to do,” she says. In practice, that can mean adding foot mobility and strength drills to your routine and choosing shoes that let your toes spread naturally.

Perez favors Altra Fit, both for her own footwear and when recommending shoes to others, because it gives the forefoot more room than a traditionally tapered toe box. Conley’s experience shows how the amount of cushioning that feels right can change over time as your foot gets stronger and needs more targeted footwear. She started out in the Altra FWD VIA 2, a cushioned shoe with the original (read: roomiest) FootShape™ and a 4 mm drop that felt familiar coming from conventional running shoes. “I was getting some toe splay and my foot was getting stronger,” she recalls. “Now I put them on, and it’s too much shoe for me because I don’t need as much cushioning.”

That’s where having options comes in. Altra’s Torin 9 offers a more moderate level of cushioning, standard footshape (secure midfoot), and a zero-drop platform that is good for running and still takes advantage of the Altra Fit that helps your feet get stronger as you log miles. For a lower-profile option, the Altra Escalante 5 has low cushioning, a 24 mm stack height, zero drop, and the original, roomiest FootShape fit.

“You’ll want to use the least amount of shoe assistance necessary for the activity,” Perez recommends. A lower-profile, more flexible shoe, like the Escalante 5, offers more ground feel for strength training, while extra cushioning or rocker geometry, found in the Torin 9 and FWD VIA 2, may be useful on longer runs. Conley agrees that a plush running shoe isn’t necessarily the best tool for lifting. “You can’t feel the ground,” she says of maximalist shoes. “You’re standing on something that decreases your sensory acuity.”

If multidimensional fitness is new to you, Conley recommends starting with manageable strength work (two or three days a week), walking, and one or two mobility or foot exercises, and build gradually as your strength and capacity improve. “Do things that challenge you, but not to the point where you start to feel overwhelmed,” she says.

If you already work out or run regularly, consider what’s missing from your routine while prioritizing your main goal. Conley suggests making room for mobility, balance, and power work, and fitting short foot-strength and mobility exercises into existing workouts. Do it while you’re fresh, adjusting your workload when running volume increases or recovery suffers.

The goal isn’t to do everything all the time or become an expert at every type of training. It’s to build a body that can keep doing the things you love. Run the trails. Lift the heavy stuff. Hike the mountain. Get down on the floor with your kids and grandkids—and have the strength and mobility to get back up again.

#4654. Tesla stops selling every Cybertruck except the $109,990 Cyberbeast

Tesla is now only selling one version of the Cybertruck in the US: the tri-motor Cyberbeast, which just got another $7,500 price hike to $109,990.

The Dual Motor and Premium AWD trims are still listed on Tesla’s configurator, but both are greyed out and can’t be selected. So the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today costs $109,990, up 57% from $69,990 in early August.

Here’s what Tesla’s US configurator shows today with a Los Angeles delivery address:

A week ago, the Cyberbeast cost $102,490. Before that, it was $99,990. That’s a $10,000 (10%) increase in about a week on a truck that hasn’t changed: 320 miles of estimated range, 11,000 lbs of towing, and 0-60 mph in 2.6 seconds.

On November 6, the same day Elon Musk announced the end of Cybertruck production, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. That made the $92,490 Premium AWD the entry point. Now it’s gone too, with no announcement. The configurator just stopped letting you pick it.

New inventory isn’t an alternative either. When we checked, Tesla’s inventory search showed no new Cybertrucks within 200 miles of Los Angeles.

This comes two days after Musk extended Cybertruck production through the end of summer 2027 to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” On Monday, he claimed the order rate “far exceeds” production and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.”

If there really is a backlog, cutting off the two cheaper trims is one way to cap it before the line shuts down. It also pushes whatever demand is left toward the most expensive, highest-margin version of the truck.

But the sales data doesn’t describe a truck with a demand problem in the other direction. We estimate Tesla delivered 7,000 to 8,000 Cybertrucks in Q3, a pace of about 30,000 a year on a line with more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. And in February, Tesla was offering a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 for “only the next 10 days.”

That’s $50,000 less than the cheapest Cybertruck you can order today. Nine months later.

Some of those $59,990 buyers are still waiting on delivery dates pushed into 2027. Tesla hasn’t said whether their orders, or any other Dual Motor and Premium orders in the queue, will be built before production ends.

Unlike the thousands of $59k CT orders that may never get manufactured I can guarantee that every high margin $110k CyberBeast order will be delivered before production ends.

This is the wind-down playbook, and it’s moving faster than I expected. Announce the end, raise prices, pull the cheaper trims, and sell the last trucks in their most expensive form. Tesla is squeezing as much as it can out of every remaining Cybertruck.

I don’t blame Tesla for wanting margin on a program it’s walking away from. But it makes the “order backlog” talk look like what we said it was: an end-of-life rush Tesla created by announcing the end, now being monetized with a $109,990 sticker. Not great for anyone who was told in 2019 that this truck would start at $39,900, or that the tri-motor version would cost $69,900.

If you want a Cybertruck that isn’t a Cyberbeast, you’re now shopping used. And I’d keep an eye on used prices, because a truck that’s going out of production with no cheaper new option could hold its value better than it has over the last two years.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4652. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”
