#4495. The Unintended Consequences of Good Intentions

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

I was intrigued to read a recent article about honeybees aggressively bumping bumblebees out of the way when they alit on the same flowers, mercilessly chasing them off.1

It is a story of unintended consequences. Apparently, the number of registered beekeepers more than doubled between 2010 and 2025, following campaigns encouraging us to get involved in saving endangered insects. Now it seems that this growth in honeybees is having harmful, unforeseen effects on other wild pollinators.1

It happens so often, doesn’t it? Someone, often a politician, presents what seems a commonsense or creative idea to better a bad situation, then someone else calmly points out all the downsides that just haven’t been thought of.

We are so focused on whatever has our attention that we don’t see the big picture, leaving us in tunnel vision.

It is something that human givens therapists stay alert to at all times. When our clients focus on a particular view or sense of understanding, we can stay neutral, stand back, and bring attention to elements that they cannot see.

For instance, a client once consulted me about her plan to write a will leaving her worldly goods to just two of her three adult children. She loved them all equally and, on the face of it, her plan seemed logical. Her elder daughter had a lucrative job in finance while her younger daughter was a struggling actor and her son a struggling musician. I pointed out that while her plan made monetary sense, she wasn’t taking into account the potential emotional meaning of leaving money in a will.

Screenwriter, TV producer and novelist Daisy Goodwin has written about this. With her highly successful TV career, she had no financial worries and could accept that her siblings had greater need of the proceeds of their mother’s estate when she died. Her mother left Daisy just a small cash sum and some personal items and wrote in her will, “I leave my daughter Daisy out of the estate not because I love her any less but because I think she has less need of it.”

Daisy’s response? “But, and here’s the rub, although I know in my head that my mother’s will is fair, in my heart I feel left out. I love my siblings dearly, and I don’t begrudge them the money; I can understand they need it more than I do, but all the same I feel rejected. I am pretty sure that this was not my mother’s intention; she was trying to do the right thing as she saw it, but the result left me, a decade later, still trying to fight the feeling that she left me out of her will because she loved me less.”2

It is a good example of seeing just part of the picture and thinking others will view things as we do. Often, in such cases, what is conceived in generosity ends up causing unforeseen rifts in the family.

Michael was devastated when a presentation he had spent his personal time on was rejected without explanation. He had had “a revolutionary idea” that, he believed, would reposition the company in a way that would drive a host of new clients to them. He expected his bosses to be as excited as he was and arranged a meeting with the chief executive officer and second-in-command to demonstrate his vision in a dramatic video, packed with punch.

To his astonishment, his presentation was met with silence. Then he was politely thanked and told that “they would think about it.” Eventually, he received an email saying the company would not be pursuing his idea.

What Michael had entirely ignored in his single-minded focus on his vision were perspectives other than his own. His bosses felt undermined, and that the current approach, which they had masterminded, was being disrespected. Instead of taking into account their need for a sense of status and achievement, he had ridden roughshod over their ideas, expecting them to receive this gladly. The irony is that they probably all lost out. It was a honeybee manoeuvre, with no good outcome for anyone, when, correctly thought through and introduced gradually, outcomes might have been very different.

When we want to bring about change, we may have only the best of intentions. But we have to bring others with us, including critics or those who may be affected in ways that they don’t initially like. Putting ourselves in others’ shoes and foreseeing unwanted outcomes remain the unmissable first steps in all such circumstances.

#4494. Nearly 3 million pages of military records from the War of 1812 are finally online

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 2:01 PM EST

After 16 years of painstaking work, the National Archives and its collaborators have finally completed digitizing over 90,000 pension applications submitted to the United States government following the War of 1812. The project is more than just preservation for preservation’s sake. The roughly 2.8 million pages contain long-forgotten and missing details about 19th century Americans, their families, and their everyday lives.

While archivists previously digitized a similar collection related to the American Revolutionary War, the new documents will help fill in knowledge gaps between early 19th century military events and the 1850 federal census. Patricia Oxley, president of the Federation of Genealogical Societies (FGS), explained the project was also incredibly time-sensitive.

“In the specific case of the War of 1812 pension records, there is an added priority due to their frail state where not acting may mean sacrificing these for future generations,” Oxley said in a recent announcement.

The somewhat new United States of America declared war on the United Kingdom on June 18, 1812, citing objections to trade restrictions with France amid the Napoleonic Wars, as well as the Royal Navy’s impressment of American sailors. Although the conflict famously included a British attack on Washington D.C. that resulted in the burning of the White House and U.S. Capitol, little shifted geopolitically between the two nations following the ratification of the Treaty of Ghent on February 17, 1815. The U.S. tallied around 15,000 casualties, while the U.K. and Canada saw about 10,700 deaths. Another 9,000 Indigenous fighters died while enlisted between the two sides.

Today’s military records are meticulously documented and stored digitally, but applying for benefits such as pensions was a much more labor-intensive process during the 19th century. With the burden of proof on each applicant, veterans were required to supply lengthy accounts of their service. Each War of 1812 pension file is liable to contain not just combat information, but the names and personal details of fellow soldiers, family members, spouses, and countless other relations.

“Our users have been asking for the War of 1812 pension records for some time, and I expect this collection to be very popular based on the rich war time detail it contains,” added Brian Hansen, general manager at Fold3, Ancestry’s military records service and National Archives collaborator.

The collection also includes a full-text search feature using handwriting recognition technology. This lets users explore the files based on every named individual, and not simply the primary veteran applicants. The pension records are currently available for free on Fold3’s website, and are being added to the National Archives catalog on a rolling basis.

Correction 11/20/26 9:30 a.m. EST: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated the pension archive contained around 7 million files. This was based on an initial assessment from researchers in 2010. The article has been updated to reflect the more accurate tally.

#4493. Current classics: Lord mayor of London’s limo latest to go electric

If you wake up tomorrow as the esteemed Lord Mayor of London, you’ll want to make a properly dignified entrance. To make sure your arrival turns the right heads, Electrogenic has taken the Mayor’s 1973 Roll-Royce Phantom VI and turned it into a properly traditional standard-bearer with modern electric power.

The stately, stylish, and silent electric Rolls-Royce car made its public debut at last month’s Salon Privé weekend at Blenheim Palace, where it joined a growing fleet of classic Rollers that have received Elctrogenic’s electric conversion, including the stunning Mulliner-bodied 1929 Phantom II that we covered back in 2023.

For this project, Electrogenic carefully removed the internal combustion-based engine, transmission, and fuel system from the City of London Corporation’s official ’73 Phantom VI limo and replaced it with a 120 kW (~160 hp) electric motor putting out 310 Nm (~230 lb-ft) of torque. Sharp-eyed readers will note those numbers are significantly lower than what you’d expect from the 6.2L L410 V8 fitted with twin SU carburetors (as it was in the standard ’73 IV), but since those numbers were never officially published, we would say that the power available from the new electric drivetrain is similarly adequate for Mayoral use.

Power for the electric motor comes from a 62 kWh li-ion battery fitted under the hood bonnet, and offers more than enough range to get the Lord Mayor to their appointments in and around the city.

To ensure the heads of the heads of the city don’t bob in an undignified manner while on parade, Electrogenic added a “ceremonial” drive mode that trims power and torque and softens the throttle map, so the chauffeur can more easily hold the crawling pace demanded by civic processions and state occasions.

“We were honored to be asked to electrify this significant motor car, and to play a part in the City of London Corporation’s journey to net zero,” says Steve Drummond, chief executive of Electrogenic. “When it was launched in the late 1960s, the Rolls-Royce VI was the most refined and dignified limousine on the road. Now, thanks to electrification, its core character has been enhanced further: it is whisper quiet, effortless to drive with swift performance, and emits zero tailpipe emissions.”

It's important for government to be seen to follow it's own policy.

The Phantom was converted as part of the Corporation’s broader effort to achieve a net zero carbon emissions goal from its own operations in 2027.

#4492. High Fat Diet Linked to Higher Colon Cancer Risk, Early Research Shows

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new study, researchers report that a high fat diet may potentially increase the risk of colon cancer.

The researchers from Arizona State University said a diet high in certain fats can cause lasting changes in intestinal stem cells that lead to the development of tumors and the possibility of colon cancer.

The study was conducted in mice, but the researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may explain their growth and survival.

The researchers published their findings on November 12 in the journal Stem Cell Reports.

The researchers said the study is important because 1 in 25 people develop colon cancer in their lifetime. In the United States, that translates into about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer every year. About 55,000 males and 55,000 females are expected to die from the disease in 2026.

Experts not involved in the study say the research provides valuable information, but they have reservations about the results, as the findings do not yet apply to humans.

“The findings provide a potential mechanism linking diet to intestinal cancer development, but we need to be cautious about translating these results to humans,” said Dalia Perelman, MS, CDE, a research dietitian at Stanford University in California.

“We already have evidence from human studies that obesity and certain dietary patterns, particularly those high in processed meats and low in fiber-rich foods, are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk,” Perelman told Healthline. “This study adds a potentially important mechanism to investigate, but it does not establish that dietary fat itself increases colorectal cancer risk in humans.”

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, shared similar views.

“This study provides a better understanding at the cellular level of how a high fat diet may contribute to colorectal cancer development,” Thanki told Healthline.

“Animal studies are an important starting point for understanding biological processes, but we must be cautious about directly applying their findings to humans,” he added. “Mice and humans share many cellular and biological mechanisms, which makes these studies valuable in identifying potential pathways involved in disease development. However, human diets, genetics, metabolism, and environmental exposures are more complex.”

To reach their findings, the Arizona State researchers fed mice what the scientists described as a Western-style high fat diet for 6 months.

They then compared those results with those from mice given a low fat diet.

The researchers said the mice on the high fat diet gained more weight than the mice on the low-fat diet. They also developed more intestinal stem cells, and those cells grew at a more rapid rate.

They added that mice genetically predisposed to intestinal cancer who were fed a high-fat diet developed more and larger tumors.

The researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may help explain their increased growth and survival.

They also pointed out that stem cell behavior returned to normal after high fat diet mice were switched to a low fat diet, although some DNA changes persisted. After four weeks, approximately 18% of these changes remained.

When mice were returned to a high fat diet, the researchers said their intestinal stem cells responded more quickly and strongly than those of mice exposed to the diet for the first time.

They concluded that the study suggests that maintaining a healthy, low fat diet may help regulate intestinal stem cell growth and reduce colon cancer risk.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, RD, president of KAK Consulting and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Ohio, wasn’t involved in the study but highlighted a particular aspect of the findings.

“What I found particularly interesting was that even after the mice returned to a low fat diet, some of the molecular changes persisted,” she told Healthline. “This raises questions about how our dietary patterns over time may influence long-term health.”

Experts said these new findings are interesting but noted numerous caveats.

“One important takeaway is that dietary habits over time matter,” said Thanki. “Even if someone has consumed a high fat diet for years, making changes now may still provide meaningful health benefits.”

“I also think these findings are particularly important for children and adolescents, as establishing healthier dietary habits early in life may provide long-term benefits,” he added.

However, Thanki noted that not all fats are the same. “The health risks depend partly on the type of fat consumed, how much is consumed, and what foods make up the overall diet,” he said.

“Diets consistently high in saturated fats, particularly those containing large amounts of processed meats, fried foods, and highly processed products, can contribute to obesity, elevated cholesterol, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction. These factors can also contribute to chronic inflammation and may increase the risk of certain cancers, including colorectal cancer,” Thanki continued.

Perelman said the diet used in the study was extremely high in fat, providing 60% of calories from fat, primarily from lard.

“We know that the health effects of dietary fats differ depending on their sources and fatty acid composition, and we cannot assume that a diet rich in unsaturated fats from foods such as olive oil, nuts, and seeds would produce the same effects,” she noted.

Perelman added that the researchers primarily studied stem cells from the small intestine rather than the colon.

“Although these tissues share some biological characteristics, they have important differences, and we cannot assume that the same changes would occur in the colon,” she explained.

Finally, Perelman noted that “the mice consuming the high fat diet also gained weight, making it difficult to separate the effects of dietary fat itself from those associated with increased body fat and other metabolic changes.”

Not all high fat foods are unhealthy. Some high fat foods that offer healthy benefits include:

“The goal shouldn’t necessarily be to eliminate fat because our bodies need healthy fats for normal functioning,” said Thanki. “Instead, people should focus on reducing saturated and trans fats while incorporating healthier unsaturated fats in appropriate amounts.”

Thanki had several dietary suggestions. Among them:

“Consistency matters more than perfection. Even modest dietary changes, maintained over time, can have meaningful health benefits,” Thanki said.

Perelman agreed. “The overall quality of the diet matters. Diets that are very high in fat may displace other foods and nutrients that have important health benefits,” she said.

“For colorectal cancer specifically, higher intakes of dietary fiber and whole grains have consistently been associated with lower risk,” Perelman noted.

“Therefore, rather than focusing exclusively on reducing fat, it is important to consider the overall dietary pattern and whether it provides adequate amounts of fiber-rich plant foods and other beneficial nutrients.”

Kirkpatrick agreed that the type of fat is what is important. “A Mediterranean-style diet that includes olive oil, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish can be relatively high in fat but is consistently associated with positive health outcomes,” she said.

“On the other hand, a diet high in saturated fat, processed meats, and ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of certain chronic diseases, particularly when it’s also low in fiber and other protective nutrients.”

Kirkpatrick also noted that many lifestyle habits contribute to a person’s overall health.

“Our health is influenced by so many factors beyond diet, including how we manage stress, our sleep habits, physical activity, genetics, and overall lifestyle,” she said.

#4491. When Saying ‘No’ to an Aging Parent Is Complicated

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Let’s start with an example: Mira*, a 78-year-old mother of two adult children, has begun to experience significant change in her physical and cognitive abilities, causing her to need more support from her oldest adult daughter, Jackie.

When Jackie was a child, her mother experienced periods of severe depression, isolating from Jackie and her younger sister, Karen, and leaving Jackie to do things like make dinner and help Karen with her homework. Their father, Stan, was often traveling for work, and Jackie felt guilty at the thought of telling him when he returned about how their mother had essentially ‘checked out’ of parenting.

Now as adults, Karen lives across the country, and Jackie, being the closest and oldest sibling, has been tasked with taking their mother to doctors’ appointments, cooking and cleaning for her, and keeping her company when her mother calls her crying. Exhausted and resentful, Jackie begins therapy to figure out how to address her need for freedom from her mother’s demands while also supporting both of her aging parents.

Parents have an uncanny ability to move us straight back into our childhood selves. Like a game of Chutes and Ladders, one look, comment, or criticism can send us sliding back down into our most painful core beliefs about ourselves, an internal drumbeat of fears that may include, Am I enough? Am I too much? Am I lovable? As parents age, they have more needs, and what was developmentally inappropriate for someone to handle in childhood becomes a more age-appropriate task of middle adulthood: Attending to the growing needs of aging parents. But behavior that was problematic for a parent when their children were young, if unaddressed, only becomes magnified as their bodies and minds begin to slow down, illnesses take over, and independence wanes. The parentified child, perhaps doing the painful and arduous therapeutic work of self-discovery over decades, is newly practiced and armed with coping tools, one of which is learning how to say no.

How do parentified adult children navigate this juxtaposition of caring for aging parents who parentified them and still maintain clarity and the ability to set much needed boundaries?

In the United States, women are the primary caregivers for an aging society, taking on the low-paying or no-paying job of care work, both formally in the healing professions and informally within their families. As demonstrated by a recent and all-too-accurate skit on SNL, the majority of caregiving falls to women, and in the case of aging parents, often the oldest (or most available) daughter. Health, education, and literacy occupations (also known as HEAL) have long been viewed as ‘women’s work,’ and broad societal attitudes such as these have trickled down and influenced our social norms, creating the expectation for women to be more flexible, more generous with their time, and more understanding of the hardship that caregiving can create.

The weight of ingrained societal and familial expectation, the feelings of guilt for having needs and setting boundaries, and the effort to resist fixing and taking responsibility can be heavy and overwhelming. Developing a plan to manage your feelings in the day-to-day interactions with an aging parent is helpful. The next time you find yourself caught in the cycle of blame, shame, guilt, and resentment related to caregiver duties, think about the following:

The ‘no’ is complicated, especially for women. It comes with the weight of societal expectations, cultural considerations, and years of history between family members. Given this, I want to encourage setting the boundary that feels right for you at any given time. One day, it might look like not picking up the phone or returning a call until you feel ready. Another day, it might involve being proactive and stopping by before a crisis occurs. Whatever it is, know that if you attune to your own feelings and needs first, your inner compass will guide you to your best solution in that moment.

* Disclaimer: This is a composite example that captures the spirit of the many iterations of similar situations that I have seen over the years in my practice. It does not refer to any one specific situation or person/people.

#4490. Where is bald eagle Kaydee? Shadow’s pal has avoided the nest.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 2:13 PM EST

Turn off reality TV and turn on the bald eagle cams. It’s all the drama you need.

When internet-famous bald eagle Shadow seemingly welcomed a mysterious new female into his nest earlier this week, many fans have questioned the whereabouts of Kaydee. After the death of Shadow’s longtime partner Jackie in August, he had been spotted spending time with the 4-year-old banded female eagle named KD1 (later renamed Kaydee). It seemed like the eagles might head into mating season as a pair, but after the arrival of a new, large female, it’s unclear how the relationships will all shake out.

Since the appearance of the mystery female, nicknamed Big Beautiful Visitor or BBV by some fans, Kaydee has disappeared from view of Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV)’s two cameras. She was last spotted by the cameras on November 14 in the Roost Tree, according to FOBBV. Despite concerns that she may be injured or had left the area, wildlife photographers have continued to document Kaydee’s presence near Big Bear Lake as recently as November 18.

Photographer Alla Shumko shared photos of Kaydee perched near Big Bear Lake on November 18. Kaydee’s double bands are visible as she observed a scuffle between younger eagles fighting over fish.

Mating season is well underway, so viewers of FOBBV’s 24/7 livecams have been watching closely for signs that Shadow has selected a new partner. Shadow has worked with both Kaydee and the new eagle on nest maintenance and shared “beaky kisses” with each female, both signs of bonding in bald eagles. Bald eagle mating involves a bit of aerial acrobatics—copulating pairs can be seen in what’s called a “cartwheel display,” in which they lock talons in mid-air while tumbling down to the ground. Male eagles do not have an external phallus, so mating occurs via a touch of cloacas. Vocalizations can typically be heard during the act, which lasts about 7 to 12 seconds, according to Raptor Resource.

As this is nature, we humans can’t predict or influence who Shadow will pick as a new partner. Or if he picks at all. All we can do is watch and wait and let nature take its course.

#4489. BYD’s luxury SUV pulled a nearly 400,000-pound jumbo jet on just two wheels [Video]

Most SUVs are lucky to tow a small trailer without breaking a sweat. BYD’s new luxury SUV had a slightly bigger challenge: pulling a nearly 400,000-pound jumbo jet. And somehow, it did it on just two wheels. The video is worth a look.

The Bao 5 made its European debut at the Goodwood Festival of Speed (FOS) in July, the first SUV from BYD’s “premium technology-focused” brand, Denza.

As Denza’s first SUV designed specifically for Europe, Stella Li, BYD’s executive vice president, said the company is “confident that the Bao 5 will be a huge hit,” offering the perfect mix of off-road ability, luxury, and advanced technology.

The SUV uses BYD’s DMO (Dual Mode Off-road) plug-in hybrid powertrain, which BYD said is the “world’s first off-road-dedicated hybrid architecture/”

BYD’s off-road PHEV powertrain features three electric motors (one on each axle and a third generator) and a 1.5L turbocharged engine, delivering a combined 536 horsepower (544 PS) and 560 lb-ft (760 Nm) of torque.

BYD boasted that “Those figures – well clear of PHEV rivals’ and comfortably more than conventional diesel SUVs’ – are enough for a 0-100km/h time of just 4.8 seconds.”

To top it off, BYD added a double wishbone front and rear suspension with its DiSus-P intelligent body system, plus front and rear intelligent electronic differential locks with millisecond-level response to improve traction and performance.

The Bao 5 is equipped with a 31.8 kWh BYD Blade Battery that delivers a pure-electric WLTP range of up to 56 miles (90 km). And on a full tank and a full charge, the WLTP combined range is 537 miles (835 km).

To prove the new luxury SUV’s capabilities, BYD put it to the ultimate test — towing a Boeing 747 jumbo jet using just two wheels.

While pulling a 180-tonne, or nearly 400,000-pound, jumbo jet on four wheels is impressive in itself, Denza’s engineers wanted to push it further, doing something never tried before to showcase its off-road DMO technology.

The Bao 5 was put to the test at Dunsfold Aerodrome airfield in Surrey, England. It successfully pulled the jumbo jet in each of its three runs: one on four wheels, one on three, and the last on just two wheels.

Combined, the SUV towed the 747 for a total of 1,600 meters, or close to a mile, which BYD said is about four laps around a standard-size athletic track.

While a feat like this sounds impressive on paper, keep in mind that planes are designed to roll with as little resistance as possible. Top Gear pulled a 747 with a Touareg a while back. The main thing a pushback rig has is weight so that it can maintain traction. That's why BYD put nearly 10,000 lbs of ballast in the back - so it wouldn't spin its wheels on the tarmac.

It's still interesting, to be sure, especially removing two wheels.

BYD said the Bao 5 was a standard, production-spec Ultimate trim model, and the modifications were minimal.

A towing attachment was added, while the interior passenger seats were removed to make space for the 9,920 lb (4,500 kg) of ballast for the two-wheel pull test. In addition, Denza added small stabilizers to each axle so the vehicle remained balanced on two wheels.

After each run, the vehicle was inspected and confirmed to show no signs of stress on the powertrain, chassis, or tires.

The Bao 5 SUV normally has a towing capacity of over 5,500 lbs (2,500 kg), according to BYD’s Denza brand.

#4488. Can Updating Drug Memories Help Treat Cocaine Addiction?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Many people recover from addiction. One obstacle along the way is exposure to drug cues—reminders of past use such as paraphernalia, places, or people. These cues can evoke vivid memories of the drug experience, triggering craving and relapse even after long periods of abstinence. Weakening such learned responses is therefore a recovery target, especially in cocaine addiction, for which no medication has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Cue-exposure therapies pursue this goal through extinction, or presenting a drug cue again and again without the drug to form a new, competing memory. Extinction does not overwrite the original drug memory, so the learned responses tend to return over time or when the drug is encountered again. Accordingly, extinction-based therapies have had limited success in preventing relapse.

Extinction learning is guided by the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), a frontal region that tracks value, and by the amygdala, a region central to emotional learning. In cocaine addiction, we previously reported lower vmPFC activity than in healthy individuals, both during drug-cue extinction and when this learning was tested the next day. This impairment may limit therapies that rely on the region.

In our 2025 PNAS study, led by Ahmet Ceceli, we merged our expertise in addiction neuroscience with our co-author Daniela Schiller’s expertise in learning and memory. We combined two windows of opportunity, one behavioral and one pharmacological, timed to coincide.

The behavioral window is memory reconsolidation. When a stored memory is recalled, it becomes unstable for a short time and can be weakened or strengthened before it is stored again. Retrieval-extinction uses this window, presenting a brief reminder of a drug cue 10 minutes before extinction to update the original memory: The cue no longer predicts the drug.

In healthy volunteers, Schiller and colleagues showed that retrieval-extinction kept learned fear from returning, with less prefrontal involvement, as if the updated memory no longer required prefrontal control. In people with heroin or nicotine addiction, retrieval-extinction has also been associated with reduced cue-induced craving.

The pharmacological window is provided by methylphenidate, best known as Ritalin and commonly prescribed for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Like cocaine, it increases the brain messengers dopamine and norepinephrine. Taken by mouth, however, it acts more slowly, consistent with a lower potential for abuse than cocaine. It nonetheless remains a controlled stimulant with risks of misuse and addiction. In rodents, it facilitates learning-related brain plasticity and extinction.

In people with cocaine use disorder, a single low dose taken by mouth normalized prefrontal function and reduced impulsivity during a task involving drug-related words. We therefore proposed using methylphenidate not as a stand-alone treatment, but as a cognitive enhancer alongside behavioral therapies that strengthen self-control and weaken drug-related associations. Here, it was timed to peak during the reminder.

Our small proof-of-concept clinical trial included 18 adults with cocaine use disorder, 12 men and 6 women. Each took part in two identical sessions about a week apart, once after taking 20 mg of methylphenidate and once after an identical-looking placebo pill. The order was random, and neither participants nor researchers knew which pill was given. Most participants were also receiving methadone or buprenorphine for opioid use disorder.

Participants first learned to link neutral cartoon images with a brief video of someone smoking a crack pipe. A few hours later, they took the pill. One hour later, at the medication’s expected peak and inside an MRI scanner, they briefly saw some of the drug-linked images again as reminders. Ten minutes later, all images were shown repeatedly without the videos. Reminded images thus underwent retrieval-extinction, and the other drug-linked images underwent standard extinction.

The next day, participants completed a validated picture-choice task. How often they chose to view drug over pleasant pictures served as a laboratory measure of drug seeking. In our earlier work, this choice tracked current and future cocaine use.

Under placebo, vmPFC activity decreased over the course of standard extinction, replicating the impairment we previously reported in cocaine addiction. By contrast, in healthy people the vmPFC becomes increasingly engaged as standard extinction progresses, which is thought to reflect updating of the cue’s value.

On their own, the medication and the reminder each engaged the vmPFC, with the reminder only as a trend. We interpret these modest effects as a compensatory overreliance on an already compromised region.

Crucially, combining the two yielded a different pattern. When the reminder was given under methylphenidate, vmPFC activity decreased over the course of extinction, as did its communication with the amygdala. This disengagement resembles the effects of retrieval-extinction on fear memories in people without addiction, where prefrontal control may no longer be needed. It does not, however, show that the drug memory was weakened or erased.

Under placebo only, the more the vmPFC was engaged during retrieval-extinction, the more often participants chose to view drug over pleasant pictures the next day. This pattern suggests that the learned drug response persisted; it was absent under methylphenidate.

Next-day drug-picture choice did not differ significantly between methylphenidate and placebo, nor did craving or cue ratings. The findings therefore concern brain function and its relationship with behavior; they do not yet show reduced drug seeking or a treatment benefit.

To our knowledge, these results are the first to describe the brain activity underlying a combined medication-behavioral approach to drug-cue memories in human addiction. They extend memory-updating research from fear to drug memories, from animals to humans, and from behavior to the brain, while repurposing a medication already in clinical use as a cognitive enhancer.

In our impaired Response Inhibition and Salience Attribution (iRISA) model of addiction, drug cues capture excessive attention and value at the expense of other rewards, while self-control is compromised. Promoting the “forgetting” of disruptive memories may reduce drug seeking by both lowering the pull of drug cues and enhancing self-control. Similar principles may apply to other conditions marked by harmful responses to powerful memories, such as posttraumatic stress disorder.

As a proof of concept, this trial was small, tested a single dose, included no healthy comparison group, and measured behavior only on the following day. Its results await replication in larger samples that allow comparisons by sex, drug use history, and substance. Longer-term studies should also test whether repeated sessions lead to lasting normalization of prefrontal function and, ultimately, to less craving, drug seeking, and relapse.

By precisely targeting compromised prefrontal circuits, medication-enhanced cognitive training may ultimately support recovery from addiction.

A brief reminder can reopen a drug memory for updating. In this study, methylphenidate was timed to peak during the reminder, after which the cues were repeatedly presented without the drug video.

#4487. North Atlantic right whales named after Dolly Parton and Gonzo

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 3:00 PM EST

Less than 400 adult North Atlantic right whales (Eubalaena glacialis) still exist in the wild, making them one of the world’s most critically endangered species. Of those, 20 have officially received spiffy new names from conservationists at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life. The researchers curate the annual North Atlantic Right Whale Catalog, and attach personable monikers to a select few baleen cetaceans in order to more easily monitor them. This year, it’s time to wave hello to Dodo, Volcano, and Dolly.

“Naming right whales is a fun and creative activity for our research community, but it also allows an opportunity to connect with the whales on an individual level,” Amy Warren, an aquarium scientific program officer and name project coordinator, said in Anderson Cabot Center’s announcement. “It can be hard to relate to Catalog #5299, but a whale named Nibbles is bound to be memorable.”

The 2026 inductees also include Grand Slam (Catalog #3991) and Slide (Catalog #4991). The sister whales have a mother named Fenway (Catalog #2791), who was also named in honor of the Boston Red Sox. Grand Slam earned her new name thanks to her three patches of raised tissue known as callosities that resemble the bases on a baseball field. Meanwhile, Slide received their name due to the curved scar on her back that recalls someone sliding through home plate. Other right whale names this year include Goose, Donegal, and even Gonzo for the beloved Muppet.

“Although the names are intended to help researchers at sea, they also give the general public a better understanding of the individual whales,” added Caroline Mowdy, a spokesperson for Whale and Dolphin Conservation (WDC).

Collaborators at the WDC also created some lighthearted, yearbook-esque biographies for each whale. For example, Dolly (Catalog #4191), whose callosity looks strikingly similar to the late, great country singer’s larger-than-life hair, apparently loves the song, “Jolene.” Then again, who doesn’t?

“We see these whales and their families grow each year,” said Mowdy. “Knowing them makes the tragedies even more tragic, but it also makes our determination to protect them even stronger.”

On Monday, the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium announced that there are roughly 382 North Atlantic right whales, representing a 1.8 percent drop in population size from the 2024 estimate. Their primary threats remain getting tangled in fishing line and vessel strikes.

However, even amid their struggles, the 2025–2026 right whale calving season saw the most calves born since 2009. A total of 24 calves were born, including a surprising late addition that was spotted in Canada in September.

#4486. Volvo EWR150 Electric wheeled excavator gets to work in Luxembourg

As no-drip, low-noise job sites become more the global rule rather than the exception, Volvo’s incredibly versatile EWR150 Electric wheeled excavators are proving to be a smart addition to construction and municipal fleets – that’s proving true in Luxembourg, as well.

The Volvo EWR150 Electric wheeled excavator is helping the postage stamp nation of Luxembourg connect natural freshwater springs to a planned water reservoir, but the work has to be done in an existing groundwater protection zone, where even the smallest fuel spills or oil leaks could have serious consequences. An ideal opportunity, in other words, for a battery electric machine like the EWR150 Electric to shine.

“Sometimes I miss the sound of the engine,” says Thomas Weber, an operator on the project who’d previously worked with the conventional EWR150 wheeled excavator. “But the quieter operation of the EWR150 Electric is more beneficial for me, personally. Compared to the diesel equivalent, I find the performance and power to be identical.”

Volvo CE took to LinkedIn to share the work being done by the Luxemburgers at construction firm Elenz, touting the Volvo’s clean, quiet running in this highly environment.

For their part, Elenz executives are equally excited about the new machine. “Going electric is not a regulation, but a requirement for this particular job,” explains Christoph Schommer, Managing Director of Elenz. “We are thoroughly impressed by the EWR150 Electric. Its low noise level is a major advantage here. At the same time, the machine offers plenty of power and consistently delivers the same level of energy.”

The EWR150 Electric is built around a 270 kWh, 600V li-ion battery pack powering an electric drive motor that’s backed by a KERS-style hydraulic boom energy-recovery system that works like regenerative braking to extend the machine’s operating time. A 0.67 m³ (~0.9 yd³) bucket with 108.5-kN (~ 24,390 lb.) breakout force is standard, and offers a, 8.95 meter (~29 foot) maximum digging reach and 5.23 meter (~17 foot) digging depth. Volvo says the machine can typically operate for 8–10 hours depending on the application

Elenz is charging their EWR150 Electric overnight using a 32A L2 connection at a nearby sewage treatment plant, which also serves as the project office and a secure parking location for site equipment. By charging overnight, when Elenz’ crew isn’t working, the company has been able to integrate the big BEV without changing their existing work schedules.

#4485. How Kelly Rowland Keeps Her Eczema Flare-Ups Under Control During Winter

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Wintertime can bring everyone down with its colder weather and less sunlight. But for those with eczema, this time of year can wreak havoc on their skin, too.

That’s the case for Grammy-winning singer, actress, and Destiny’s Child alum Kelly Rowland, who has been living with eczema since her 20s. During the winter months, she often dreads the cold.

“[You] don’t know what the environment is going to give you—because mine is also environmental—or what the weather is going to give you,” Rowland told Healthline.

Cold weather and indoor heating can reduce humidity, drying out the skin and triggering or worsening eczema flare-ups.

“[What we know] about the skin barrier is that it really is like a gate or wall against the outside world,” Camille Howard-Verovic, MD, a dermatologist at Active Dermatology, told Healthline.

In healthy skin, the barrier controls what enters and leaves the skin. However, for people with eczema, Howard-Verovic said they have skin barrier dysfunction, which allows substances such as allergens and irritants to penetrate the skin.

Cold weather can increase transepidermal water loss, a process in which moisture escapes through the skin’s outer barrier and evaporates into the surrounding air.

“People with eczema have a tremendous amount of transepidermal water loss, so you’re just drier,” said Howard-Verovic. “[You’re] not holding onto the water as well, so that causes the itching and the rash that we feel when we have eczema.”

Rowland first noticed eczema flares behind her ears as well as on her elbows, arms, and the back of her knees.

“[It] looked like a rash, so that’s what I thought it was all this time, and I dealt with it for so long until after I had my son and then it started to get worse on my face,” she said.

She eventually went to a dermatologist who diagnosed her with moderate-to-severe eczema, a chronic inflammatory skin condition that can cause intense itching, painful skin cracking, thickened skin, and redness or swelling.

When Rowland learned that eczema can be genetic, it made sense to her.

“I remember seeing big rashes on [my mom’s] neck and her arms…so she had it, and I guess I was the lucky one,” said Rowland.

At first, she tried eliminating foods that she thought might be triggers. She also bathed in oatmeal.

“[I] literally have had a tub full of oatmeal, like literally went to the store to get store-bought fresh oats,” she said. “I tried everything, and it doesn’t help until you go talk to a doctor about it.”

At first, she tried prescription topical medications but found them cumbersome.

“I don’t have the time, if I’m being honest, and we live in a world that is moving so fast…I started buying like three tubes of whatever it was I was using and losing it; it was just too much for me,” Rowland said.

Rowland said she found relief with Ebglyss, a prescription injectable medication for moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. She has also partnered with Eli Lilly and Company, its manufacturer, to raise awareness about eczema.

Rowland said she’s sharing her experience to help others living with eczema, including people she’s met who have experienced greater challenges managing the condition.

“One lady was telling me about how she’s having a tough time [looking] in the mirror cause she doesn’t know who’s looking back at her, and she saw her skin before eczema and after,” said Rowland.

When she first had symptoms, she said she felt embarrassed, too.

“[Because] it was just in the middle of my arm space and…[if I] put out my hand to shake someone’s hand, you don’t know if somebody’s judgy,” she said.

Rowland hopes being open about her condition will encourage others to advocate for themselves and talk with their doctor about treatment options.

Because eczema can look different on deeper skin tones, Howard-Verovic noted that a dermatologist can help make the correct diagnosis.

“Some people may not even know that they have eczema,” she said. “We know that eczema is a rash; it can appear red on certain skin tones, and it can be grey or white on certain skin tones, so it can look a little different.”

In addition to medication, Rowland said managing stress helps reduce her eczema flare-ups.

“Before [when] I went on tour, because I was under so much stress, it flared up like crazy, like you wouldn’t believe,” she said. “We were in the back trying to figure out how to cover certain things up, and we figured some of it out, and some of it was really tricky, but what helped was when I actually just calmed down…not that it helped overnight, but it did just kind of bring the flare down.”

She said red light therapy, feeling grounded outside without her shoes on, getting vitamin D from natural sunlight, and cooking are ways she reduces ongoing stress.

“Cooking calms me when my kids aren’t here, and I have a really good [Zen] playlist on,” said Rowland. “[If] you ask me a question [in those moments], I might give you my heart; I’m just so happy.”

She also tries to cut back on sugar, which she believes triggers flares.

Another way to reduce flares, according to Howard-Verovic, is to avoid hot showers, especially in the winter.

“[We] know eczematous skin likes lukewarm water,” she said.

Because Howard-Verovic and her daughter both live with eczema, she set a rule about when it’s time to get out of the shower.

“[If] you see condensation on the bathroom mirror, you’ve spent too much time in the shower,” said Howard-Verovic. “[That] really hot, hot water feels really good in that moment…but when you get out all that water evaporates, and there’s no moisture in the atmosphere, and it dries your skin out, and now your skin is unhappy again.”

If you prefer to take baths, she said use gentle cleansers.

“[There] are bleach baths for really, really bad flare-ups,” she noted.

Diluted bleach baths are sometimes recommended for people with eczema, but they should only be used according to a healthcare professional’s instructions.

As soon as you get out of the shower or bath, Howard-Verovic said to apply a quality moisturizer to your damp skin. According to the National Eczema Association (NEA), lotions containing the following ingredients can help ease dry skin associated with eczema.

To help identify appropriate products, look for ones that have the NEA’s Seal of Acceptance.

#4484. Pleasure Is Medicine: The Legacy of Beverly Whipple

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

My dear friend, mentor, and pioneer in the field of human sexuality, Dr. Beverly Whipple, has died. To pay tribute, I want to fully communicate how her contributions to the field rocked the world. I want to celebrate the huge impact she had in legitimizing women’s pleasure so that women themselves would be encouraged to explore their bodies and their pleasure capacity. Beyond her groundbreaking book, The G Spot and Other Discoveries about Human Sexuality, Beverly single-handedly blazed a trail that led to some of the biggest breakthroughs in human sexuality research in our lifetime. But I also want to share the life lessons I had the privilege of learning in my relationship with her.

I’m having a conversation with Beverly in my mind. As I struggle to get this tribute right, I hear her say, “Relax, just do a good-enough job!” She taught me and others not to strive so hard. To let go of being goal-directed in bed. To not pursue “great sex” in lieu of enjoying the good-enough sex we were already having, while remaining open to exploring more. Beverly’s guidance is why my book, Why Good Sex Matters, isn’t titled Why Great Sex Matters. I loosen and soften as words and tears flow.

I pause. My last blog was about grief over losing my pet. The loss-of-a-dear-friend-and-mentor grief has only made the lessons loom larger. I trust Beverly would agree: To be fully alive, we need to feel the full range of our emotions, both painful and pleasurable.

Life is full of joy and loss, and the biggest loss is not to feel it all. And pleasure, both in and out of the bedroom, is medicine. It makes our brain and bodies work better and makes life worth living. (Click here to read her paper on the benefits of sexual expression on physical health.)

Beverly had a relentless curiosity and amazing ability to observe and listen. As a nursing student, when asked by patients if they could resume sex after a heart attack, her supervisor met her questions with a blank stare; she saw the huge gaps in knowledge about sexuality. Then later, as a nursing instructor, when she tried to teach about human sexuality and was told not to do so, she promptly left to develop a sexual health curriculum to teach elsewhere.

In the 1970s, she taught women with urinary incontinence Kegel exercises to strengthen the pelvic floor. She listened when some reported that stimulation of a sensitive area on the front wall of the vaginal wall was associated with intense pleasure and the release of fluid, and she got curious. While the medical field was quick to dismiss this as urinary incontinence, Beverly dug up a 1950 paper by a pioneering gynecologist, Dr. Ernst Gräfenberg, who was the first to identify this “erotic” zone and describe the ejaculate released from stimulation of this region.

She began work with sex researcher Dr. John Perry to investigate this phenomenon, publishing papers and eventually the book, The G Spot, naming it after Gräfenberg. In later years, she expanded the idea of a “G spot” to what is now known as the clitourethrovaginal complex, an interconnected system including the internal clitoris, urethra, and vagina that work together during the sexual response.

But this was only the beginning of her journey. Bevely listened to women who reported being able to reach orgasm without any physical stimulation at all, through “imagery” (informally called “thinking off”). This led her to partner with my Ph.D. mentor, Dr. Barry Komisaruk, complete her own Ph.D., and conduct a study of women who reported being able to have imagery-induced orgasms. The results supported that for these women, imagery-induced orgasms produced physical changes comparable to those of orgasms from physical stimulation.

Years later in my Ph.D. studies, inspired and supported by Beverly, my colleagues and I found that when women simply “imagined” erotic genital stimulation, their brains lit up areas that register actual physical touch, along with many of the same regions that get activated during orgasm. This supports the notion that the brain or mind is the most important sex organ of all.

Beverly continued to her work and listened to women with complete spinal cord injuries who reported that they still experienced menstrual cramps and orgasm, despite doctors telling them it was medically impossible and “all in their heads.” In 2004, Beverly and Barry conducted the world’s first-ever brain imaging study of female orgasm. The results suggested that these sensations reached the brain through the vagus nerve, a cranial nerve that runs from the cervix and uterus directly to the brain, bypassing the spinal cord.

Not all people with spinal cord injury report genital sensations, but for those who do, this validated their experience and paved the way for further brain imaging research on genital stimulation and orgasm, which I had the privilege to conduct and publish for my own dissertation. That work revealed that genital stimulation and orgasm activated widespread regions of the brain, including areas involved in sensation, movement, reward, emotion, and thinking. Thus, we conclude that orgasm is a whole-brain event.

During stimulation and orgasm, oxygen-rich blood is drawn to the widespread brain regions that become activated. A well-oxygenated brain is likely a happy, healthy brain. My research also showed that many of the regions that produce, respond to, or release feel-good, good-for-you substances such as dopamine, serotonin, opioids, and endocannabinoids are active during the sexual response and orgasm.

In Beverly’s work on the health benefits of sexual expression, she pointed to research linking it to pain relief, lower stress, better sleep, and enhanced quality of life. She viewed pleasure as part of health. Our subsequent studies support this: pleasure is medicine. As I like to say, healthy hedonism heals.

Beverly was a brilliant scientist, educator, and mentor. Most of all, she was a beautiful, kind, loving human being. In tribute to her, I put together a short reel of our lab’s work, as shown on Nightline, Discovery, and other networks, as part of her legacy. She appears in the first clip, right there in the lab with us, and the work documented in the other clips all grew from the questions she asked decades ago. (Watch the reel here.)

Rest in pleasure, dearest Beverly. You live on in our hearts and our work.

#4483. New electric comb from China regrew nearly 100% of hair (in mice)

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 4:10 PM EST

A potentially revolutionary electronic comb is generating some pretty hair-raising results. The experimental comb has been used to successfully restore nearly all the hair in bald test subjects. But don’t chuck out that Rogaine just yet. The comb’s users were mice with shaved backs.

Though the Detangle comb (named after the 2010 Disney film Tangled) hasn’t been tested on humans yet, the Chinese scientist behind its development says the eye-grabbing results on our distant genetic cousins suggest it could play a role in the neverending quest to keep those luscious locks just a hair longer.

Created by a team led by Beihang University in Beijing, the comb initially looks like the chunky plastic kind adorning typical pharmacy aisles. However, a closer look at its clear plastic handle reveals a green circuit board. Further down, one can see electrodes embedded in the comb’s teeth, which alternate between long and short. The team says that this height variance makes the comb’s pulsed electric field more than two and a half times stronger than it would be with evenly matched teeth.

The shorter teeth also contain two experimental genetic treatments. One boosts blood vessel growth around the hair follicles. The other treatment  blocks dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a hormone known to shrink follicles. The electric field generated by the comb temporarily opens up skin so the treatments can get inside, reaching up to nine times deeper into the follicle region than a conventional cream.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

Researchers performed a variety of tests on mice that had their backs shaved and were given testosterone to mimic pattern baldness. Over 28 days, the balding mice were treated with minoxidil or finasteride (the current standards for medical hair restoration), the comb’s electrical stimulation alone, and the comb combined with an experimental genetic treatment. Mice given finasteride regrew about 50 percent of their hair, while the ones on and minoxidil regrew 70 percent. Those numbers  honestly aren’t  too bad on their own, but the results were even better when Detangle got involved. Mice treated with the comb and both experimental treatments saw a staggering 97.85 percent hair regrowth. And all without having to book a flight to Turkey for a hair transplant.

“[T]hese results demonstrate that electrostimulation via the Detangle system promotes hair growth and follicle regeneration in a safe and effective manner,” the team wrote in their paper published earlier this month in the Nature Communications.

The potential market for a hair regrowing comb is sizable to say the least. Detangle’’s creators say androgenetic alopecia, the scientific term for pattern baldness, affects 1.5 billion people worldwide. Some studies suggest up to 80 percent of men will experience pattern baldness, with  some populations seeing symptoms before the age of 40. Somewhere between one fifth and two fifths of women may also experience pattern hair thinning. And hair isn’t just hair. Social expectations and norms around hair partly explain why hair loss can carry psychological baggage.

Scientists and hair care providers know this, of course. Toupees, tonics, and tinctures promising to reverse nature’s balding date back thousands of years. Today, the standard medical treatment usually involves topical minoxidil (the active ingredient in Rogaine) and oral finasteride. Minoxidil generally works, but results vary widely from person to person and it requires constant, ongoing application.

Finasteride is often far more effective, with long-term studies showing it can preserve hair in most men for at least a decade, but it also carries the risk for much more intense side effects. The drug (which saw a surge in popularity thanks to online, telehealth services) has been linked to decreased libido and erectile dysfunction. Some patients have also reported anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts. While the side effects are uncommon, the risk presented a potentially steep trade off for a fuller head of hair.

Those intrigued by the comb will unfortunately have to hold out quite a bit longer. The team says more research is needed before the device is tested on humans and, even then, there’s no guarantee the rodent results will translate. Testosterone-induced hair loss on a shaved mouse back is a far cry from human pattern baldness, which typically creeps in over years.

It’s also worth emphasizing that the electric comb, memorable as it is, wasn’t solely responsible for the best results. The pair of experimental genetic treatments used in the study (called SRD5A2 siRNA and VEGFA plasmids) also need to be tested in humans to ensure they are safe and don’t come with unintended side effects of their own. Wig stores, it seems, will live to see another day.

#4482. Tesla’s Semi Megacharger network hits 7 sites, far short of 37 goal

Tesla has opened its first Semi Megacharger in Texas, an 8-stall station in Mesquite on the east side of Dallas. With it, Tesla’s map now lists 7 public Megacharger sites and 44 stalls for its electric truck.

That’s progress. But with six weeks left in 2026, it’s less than a fifth of the 37 sites Tesla planned to have open this year.

Tesla Charging announced the new station on X on Tuesday night with its usual one-liner and a photo of the stalls at sunset:

New Tesla Megacharger: Mesquite, TX (8 stalls) https://t.co/UsCFMyCjo7 pic.twitter.com/W4G1e2BHkb

Tesla’s map lists the site at 2175 S Town East Blvd in Mesquite, with eight Megachargers rated at up to 1.2 MW each.

Texas is where Tesla has the most riding on this network. When Tesla added 64 Megacharger locations to its map in February, Texas got 19 of the 66 planned sites, more than any other state. Mesquite is the first of them to go live, and several other Dallas–Fort Worth sites are still marked “coming soon.”

The Pilot truck stop rollout hasn’t reached Texas either. When Pilot opened its first Megacharger in Georgia in October, it named a Flying J in Fort Stockton, Texas, as one of the next sites. It’s still not live on Tesla’s map.

Tesla also isn’t alone in DFW. Greenlane, the truck charging joint venture between Daimler Truck, NextEra and BlackRock, announced high-power sites in Dallas and Houston in May, open to any electric truck with CCS and MCS connectors. Tesla now has a station operating in the metro.

Here’s every public Megacharger currently live on Tesla’s map:

That’s 7 sites and 44 stalls in four states. When we counted in early October, there were four customer-facing sites with 26 stalls. Tulare opened the same week, Hodgkins came on November 10, and now Mesquite.

So Tesla is adding a site roughly every two weeks.

Tesla also runs private Megachargers for its own fleet at Giga Nevada and in Carson, California, and it sells Megachargers to fleets and depot operators through its business program. Forum Mobility switched on two at the Port of Long Beach earlier this month. None of those count toward the public network that Semi buyers without their own depot rely on.

Tesla’s Q4 2025 shareholder report showed about 37 Megacharger sites for 2026. Semi program lead Dan Priestley has said Tesla wants 46 by early 2027.

To me this seems like good progress, sure it's not right on time with their ambitious goal, but they are executing on their charging network and I'm sure more sites will keep opening.

To hit 37, Tesla would need to open 30 more sites in the next 43 days. At the current pace, it ends the year with around 10.

Pilot said in October that nine more of its sites were under construction, so a late burst is possible. But it would have to be a very big one.

And the trucks are starting to show up. Tesla launched volume production of the Semi in September at a Nevada factory it says can build 50,000 trucks a year, and it said last week that Chicago’s first 50 Semis are en route for delivery, a day after Hodgkins opened. Big fleets like that customer are installing their own depot chargers anyway, and most Semi charging will happen there. The public network is what lets a Semi leave its home region.

#4481. Fiona the hippo dies at age 9

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 19, 2026 4:25 PM EST

The Cincinnati Zoo’s most famous resident Fiona the hippo has died at age 9.

“We are in shock at the moment,” Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore. Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore. She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many.”

Last week, a child’s knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remained stuck in her digestive track. She had undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that showed intestinal bunching, indicating her body was trying and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests. Just yesterday, on November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers.

“Fiona was such a gift,” said Cincinnati Zoo Executive Chair of the Board Thane Maynard. “I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle. And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”

Fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”

#4480. Amflow launches its first city e-bikes, packing huge torque and serious smart tech

Amflow has made a name for itself in the electric mountain bike world with its high-performance Avinox-powered machines, but now the company is bringing that same technology to a decidedly more urban environment. The newly unveiled Amflow UE Carbon series marks the brand’s first move into the commuter e-bike market, combining a lightweight carbon fiber frame, powerful mid-drive motor, and a surprisingly long list of smart features designed for everyday riding.

And while these might look like fairly conventional step-through city bikes at first glance, there’s some seriously impressive technology hiding beneath those clean lines.

The new Amflow UE series comes in two versions, the UE Carbon and the higher-end UE Carbon Pro, both built around a full-carbon fiber frame weighing just 2.35 kg (5.2 lb).

The complete bike weighs as little as 20.9 kg (46 lb), which is fairly impressive considering the amount of hardware Amflow has packed into it, including front suspension, a suspension dropper seatpost, integrated lighting, and cargo racks.

Both models use the Avinox M2 mid-drive motor, which delivers up to 125 Nm of torque. That’s an enormous amount of torque for a city bike, and should make short work of steep hills, especially when carrying groceries or other cargo. And to put things into perspective, a lot of city e-bikes have barely 60 Nm for torque, so Amflow is knocking it out of the park for urban power.

A removable 600 Wh battery provides a claimed maximum range of 132 km (82 miles) in the lowest power assist mode, while fast charging can refill the battery in just 2 hours and 23 minutes.

The bikes also feature Avinox’s intelligent traction control system and a new Auto Boost function that automatically provides additional assistance when the system detects demanding conditions, such as accelerating from a stop or climbing a steep hill.

In other words, riders get much of the sophisticated motor technology developed for high-performance electric mountain bikes, but in a package designed for commuting to work or picking up groceries.

The bike is listed as weighing 20.9 kg (46 lb), though that figure conveniently excludes the front and rear racks, mudguards, pedals, kickstand, bike lock, bottle cage, and chainguard. So figure a few extra pounds for all of that gear, and you’re in the right ballpark.

The main difference between the two models is their drivetrain.

The higher-end UE Carbon Pro ($3,899) uses a customized three-speed electronically shifted internally geared hub paired with a Gates carbon belt drive. That should make it particularly appealing to commuters who want a quiet, clean, low-maintenance setup without worrying about chain lubrication or derailleur adjustments.

The more affordable UE Carbon ($3,499) instead uses a 10-speed electronic derailleur developed with TRP.

Both models support automatic shifting, allowing the bike to handle gear changes without requiring the rider to constantly think about them.

Amflow has also gone fairly wild with the technology integration.

There’s a 1.4-inch touchscreen display mounted on the handlebars, a wireless phone charging mount offering 15W wireless charging or 20W USB-C charging, and integrated lighting with automatic low-light activation and brake-sensing functionality.

The bikes even include a hardened steel frame lock on the rear wheel, Apple Find My integration, and a Lost Mode feature that can lock down certain components if the bike is stolen.

Apple Watch connectivity allows riders to check their bike’s status and unlock it, while heart-rate-based assistance can automatically adjust motor output to help riders maintain a target heart rate zone.

Some of these features, like the security and tracking, are immediately effective for nearly all riders, while other high-tech features like the heart rate-based pedal assist can provide even more functionality for niche riders looking to bridge the gap between riding for transportation and riding for fitness.

Of course, all the fancy technology in the world doesn’t mean much if a commuter bike can’t handle everyday errands.

Fortunately, Amflow appears to have taken the practical side seriously.

The bikes feature a low step-through frame, upright riding position, 65 mm suspension fork, and a suspension dropper seatpost offering 125 mm of height adjustment and approximately 30 mm of suspension travel.

The 26×2.0-inch Maxxis tires should also provide a comfortable ride over less-than-perfect city streets.

There’s a front rack rated for 20 kg (44 lb) and a rear rack rated for 27 kg (59.5 lb), with the latter supporting the MIK HD mounting system for compatible accessories, including child seats.

The standard frame is designed to accommodate riders from 155 to 190 cm (5’1” to 6’3”), while a smaller version for riders down to 140 cm (4’7”) is expected in 2027.

I’ve been impressed with the technology coming out of the Avinox ecosystem, and it’s exciting to see that technology finally make its way into a more practical city-focused electric bicycle.

As much as I love high-performance electric mountain bikes, the reality is that most people aren’t spending their mornings bombing down mountain trails. They’re commuting to work, dropping kids off at school, and running errands.

And that’s where electric bicycles can make an even bigger difference.

The Amflow UE series seems to take a refreshingly comprehensive approach to urban riding. The powerful motor is nice, but I’m arguably more interested in the belt drive, integrated security, cargo capacity, automatic shifting, and built-in phone charging.

Those are the kinds of features that can make an electric bicycle genuinely easier to live with every day. And as someone who actually commutes with an e-bike each day as my main form of transportation, these bikes are really speaking to me!

If you ask me, it’s great to see another high-performance e-bike manufacturer recognizing that the future of electric bicycles isn’t just about riding farther and faster on trails. It’s also about making everyday transportation better for the less exciting type of riding, too.

#4479. It's the Time of Our Lives, Yet We Feel Time Deprived

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

We have recently gone through the semi-annual ritual of adjusting our clocks by an hour. In the spring we complain about losing an hour, and in the fall we look forward to gaining an hour, but both perceptions are an illusion. The day didn’t change at all, only the way we label it. Clearly the passage of time isn’t dependent on how we mark and measure it, and none of us know exactly how long our lives will last. But that hasn’t stopped us from worrying about it’s passage, agonizing over how to spend the time we have and debating how to track the passage of our days. A recent survey suggested that 80 percent of Americans often feel they don’t have enough time to do the things they want. The winter holiday season is unlikely to provide relief from this perceived time pressure.

Is this simply a cost of living in the modern world? In the past, feeding yourself and your family absorbed much of your time and energy, and in the pre-industrial world far fewer people had access to luxuries in life, including travel, affordable entertainment, and leisure time. While things we take for granted, including electricity, motorized transportation, the airwaves, and the internet, have made our lives easier in many ways, they have also generated their own sources of stress.

We can operate 24-hour businesses, communicate with people in distant time zones, and keep ourselves awake and wake ourselves up using the host of electronic gadgets at our disposal. No matter what we choose to do with our time off, we are consciously rejecting other options. If we go bowling, we are missing movies. If we eat out, we are choosing between multiple restaurant experiences, and staying home can feel like we are missing out on fun or useful social activities. Many of us are also struggling to keep up with the information overload endemic to modern life. No matter how we try to normalize the onslaught of advertisements, news alerts, voicemails, emails, texts, and social media notifications aimed at us through our computers and phones, keeping up is a challenge.

It doesn’t help that more than half of all Americans don’t work within the traditional 9-to-5 time frame. Around-the-clock shift work, hourly jobs, flexible and hybrid schedules, and overtime have made available a host of alternative work schedules. Although this can allow people to have more say over how they allocate their time, it also contributes to the sense that that work can too easily bleed over into our home lives. This is particularly stressful for parents attempting to meet their work and childcare commitments simultaneously.

The subjective passage of time also varies depending on what we are doing. When we are faced with a deadline, it can feel like time is flying by. When we are sick or bored, time seems to go very slowly. Likewise, time seems to go more quickly when we are happy, and too slowly when we are sad. During moments of extreme stress, our sense of time also slows, perhaps to facilitate our ability to respond to the crisis. As we age, time seems to go faster as well, perhaps because each year represents a smaller proportion of the total. While time is measurable, our perception of its passage clearly varies.

The glorification of achievement-related busyness is another problem. In the electronic age, being busy has been increasingly equated with being important, productive, and disciplined. While it is true that being gainfully employed and using time wisely can help us achieve our goals, constant pressure to produce and succeed is also associated with feelings of stress, depression, and anxiety. This rarely shows up in our social media feeds, though, as people focus on documenting their successes rather than their struggles. Nor does the cost of ignoring self-care. When faced with an overwhelming to-do list, it can be tempting to steal time from sleep, cut corners on diet and exercise, and skip social activities that might actually help us cope more effectively with the pressures in our lives.

If we can’t alter the physical passage of time or cram an unlimited number of experiences into a finite period, how can we reduce the sense that we are always out of time? The key is to change the way we think about spending time. Rather than trying to work faster, we need to accept that we can’t possibly do or experience all of the things on offer in the modern world. Instead, we need to think carefully about our priorities. How productive, meaningful, or enjoyable are the things we are doing? What would happen if we emphasized being fully present in our daily lives? The upcoming holiday might give us the opportunity. As Thanksgiving officially kicks off the holiday season, we could consciously choose to spend more time thinking about what we are doing than what we should be doing. Time itself may be limited, but our decisions about how we spend it shouldn’t be. Being mindful about how we want to spend our time is something we should all take the time to do
